articles.body: Sam Altman Talks Donald Trump, Xi Jinping, and the Risk of Extinction    Vanity Fair

scored.body: Every day a new scientific breakthrough or existential threat seems to make the world more aware and more distrusting of an AI future that we’re told is rapidly approaching—whether we like it or not.Click here for Part 1 of Vanity Fair’s Sam Altman interview.Nobody is more recognized as the face of artificial intelligence—as a technology, an industry, and a civilizational shift—than OpenAI cofounder and CEO Sam Altman, who appears at the top of our 2026 New Establishment list. (You can read the full list here, and my editor’s letter here.)In Part 1 of my interview with Sam Altman, we discuss ChatGPT and suicide prevention, “prepping” for the apocalypse, pronatalism, being portrayed by Andrew Garfield, what he really thinks of Elon Musk and Mark Zuckerberg, and being seen as the Oppenheimer of the Artificial Age.In Part 2, we cover Donald Trump, the midterms, the real risk of extinction, Xi Jinping’s state visit, self-policing versus government regulation, and OpenAI president Greg Brockman’s political donations.(OpenAI has an agreement with Condé Nast, the owner of Vanity Fair, which allows OpenAI to display its content in search results for a limited term.)Our conversations have been lightly edited for length and clarity.Watch Part 2 on this page and read the transcript below.Watch Part 1 and read the transcript here.Mark Guiducci: Sam, it’s good to see you again.Sam Altman: You too.We sat in this room three weeks ago and so much has happened since. This past week, you introduced the world to your new product, Dots. You described it as like an AI helper that always has your back inspired by the cool versions of what we watched in movies growing up. Sam, what’s a dot?Before we get to literally what it is, this is the product I have been waiting for. I like this, I think more than any product we’ve ever launched. The fact that it gets to know me as I work, the fact that it’s just kind of always working and taking on the stuff that I didn’t want to do. I noticed that, and I’m sure many other people have this too, that I let the tasks I most don’t want to deal with just pile up and pile up and it becomes this gravity well of dread and it’s just sitting there.And the fact that my dot is going through my email, going through my to-do list of just stuff that is not pleasant for me to do and where I don’t add much value and it’s just knocking that out with undefeatable spirit and energy is amazing. And I really feel like I have this thing working for me all the time.Like an assistant?It somehow feels… Assistant is the mental model that I had in mind when we started working on the product, and I think that is probably how people still are talking about it, but it feels much more like a sort of extension of me.Is it just an avatar of you? Is that a good way of thinking about it, that it knows what you want to say to those emails and is getting back to them, or…No, I think that I have figured out this good workflow where I called my dot yesterday while I had some time and I was just like, “Here’s a set of ideas.” Went off and did a bunch of work. By the time I got back to my computer, there was a bunch of things where my dot had sent me a message in Slack being like, “I did all this work. It’s bad ideas for these reasons. I also found this other stuff on your computer.” I proactively talked to three people on the team and I was like, “All right, let’s do these things and let’s keep going.” And it was just a completely new way of trying to get a new idea towards reality.I’m curious for that to be effective, it must have access to everything, because I remember we’re almost the same age. When I got to college, I immediately got on Facebook and was like… I think we were a little naive. Everyone was like free-for-all.It was a free-for-all.And no one even thought about data. How does living through Facebook impact how you think about privacy with dots particularly?We have to be extremely, extremely rigorous about privacy for this to work. But I was actually thinking about this the other day. I am kind of sad about where technology has evolved to in many ways because I feel like it is constantly taking my attention. I finally turned off almost all notifications on my phone. It’s way better, but it’s like a crazy way to live your life with your phone just buzzing at you nonstop. My hope for the world is that we’re going to automate the bad parts of life and then give people more effort, ability, time to do the good parts and express their creative spirit or push on something they care about or help their community.And in my own use, I found out that one of the things I value the most, no surprise to anyone, is these small moments of human connection. And if it’s like my dot is messaging yours and that feels really just bad, I want to send you the text.So, last time we spoke here, you were really eager to talk about Astra, the latest version of ChatGPT, but last week you delayed the latest release of Astra 6.1 after the model failed to meet safety standards. How did you come to that decision and what was Astra doing that means it’s not ready for the public?These models are in the seriously capable era now. And so, the kind of decisions where I think a year ago we could have very reasonably said, “Just put this out in the world, it’s maybe a little unsafe, but nothing that bad is going to happen and we want people to benefit from it.” It’s different now. And I think that as the capabilities continue to increase, that the bar we will hold for ourselves on safety is going to go higher and higher. Now, of course you could say, and I think some of our colleagues in the industry would say, that this stuff is just way too dangerous to release. Only a couple of companies should have it or one company or one person should have it. And that is also not right.So, there are kind of two major ways that this could go wrong. And I think the Astra 6.1 is an interesting thing to study here. You can have a big safety accident, eventually one that leads to a real loss of control where AI escapes and it’s out wreaking havoc on the internet and society can’t really get control back. AI is so much more capable than us and so smart that it’s doing things that we don’t understand and we don’t know how to stop it. This is the thing from the sci-fi movies. On the other hand, you could have AI have way too much power concentration, lead to way too much power concentration in a small number of companies or people or maybe one country.And if you don’t release at all, you can fall off that way. And again, I think there’s a lot of people are just like, “We just want the control here.” So, we have to navigate this pragmatic middle path down the center of this. And 6.1 Astra, the current model we had ready to go, I think would’ve tipped too much towards the accident risk. So, what we’re doing instead is pushing towards a model that we will still be able to distribute very broadly and we’re committed to do that even though it’s going to take a little longer, but we can make much more confident claims about the alignment.Altman and Howard Lutnick chat during the G20 Innovation Ministerial in Chapel Hill.Bloomberg/Getty ImagesSo, then this is a good example of self-regulation of saying we’re not going to release this product because we’ve determined for X, Y, Z reasons, not yet, it’s not yet safe. Which brings us to this week, President Trump and AI executives, including OpenAI's president Greg Brockman, signed an accord on superintelligence. It essentially is an agreement for the AI companies to self-regulate as I read it. I mean, it sounds like Trump wants you guys to police yourselves. You told me three weeks ago, we need our governments to step up. And then went even further the next week when you went to the UN, you said, “If AI is to be democratic, the most important decisions cannot be made by labs in San Francisco alone.” Does this new accord fall short in your view?I think it’s a good start. I think it’s much better than nothing. I remain of the belief that we are going to need more over time, but for the models of today—Because it’s kind of useless, this thing. It’s a piece of paper that has a typo on it.I don’t think that’s quite fair. I mean, yes, in some sense it has no real power. On the other hand, I think there is always social force behind these things and—It’s a gesture.…People will point to it and I think it’ll have some power inside in between these companies.What do you think is the next step that you would like to see?I think with all of these questions about next steps, we are in the realm of powerful enough models that it is difficult to predict the specific things that will go wrong in what order. And I think politics and policy is going to be very reactive to the specific things that go wrong. So, if the next big thing that goes wrong is someone makes a novel pathogen, I think that will have a very different response than if the next thing that goes wrong is more cybersecurity or people feeling like businesses can’t succeed because the model company stopped giving access.So, I think policymakers still have not really felt the exponential that we’re on, and I would guess the world in general will be caught off guard by the next thing that goes really wrong.But what’s your stance on it? Can you clarify you or your company’s position on government regulation? Because you have said, you’ve preached almost like, “Regulate us.” Sometimes the actions of the company, whether it’s lobbying in the EU or California or Greg Brockman’s political donations, don’t always seem to be aligned with that idea. So, can you clarify your stance on regulation?Yeah. I mean, this is obviously not a binary thing. I think it’s really easy for people to say either you are for all regulation or you are against all regulation. And I don’t agree with you on that framing. I think it’s very reasonable for us to say given what we see on the technology with the technology and given that we are trying to balance between these two really important things, we’re going to be in the gray area in between here. We really want people to have the technology. We really want the US to win.We really want this to be something that all people get to use and control and have a voice in the future, not just like, okay, fine, AI’s giving you a cure for cancer, but really get to use to shape where the future’s going to go. And we are willing to accept some things going wrong to make sure that this is a widely held and used and democratic technology.What do you mean by some things going wrong?I think, for example, I support open-source models. There is a coming tidal wave of cybersecurity problems that are going to come from these open-source models. Now, we’re trying to help the world be ready for that by saying we’ve got a little bit of a lead we want to help you defend, but there are people in the industry who say we should ban open source because otherwise a bunch of systems are going to be hacked. And I don’t think that price of liberty is worth it. And we’re going to, as a society, I think, have to just accept some fairly severe cyber incidents from open models in exchange for the liberty that comes with that.What’s the limit of that that we accept?I mean, that is the political process, how we determine what… Safety is always negotiated between stakeholders. Airplanes are generally thought of as very extremely safe things. Airplanes still sometimes crash. So, the limits on how much we accept for the benefits, that is not something that I think OpenAI—They’re super highly regulated.Yeah.That’s an industry with extreme regulation.Totally.Altman speaks to journalists after meeting with Hakeem Jeffries on Capitol Hill in June.BRENDAN SMIALOWSKI/Getty ImagesIn the past week or so, Jensen Huang and Bill Gates have come out as very different with different approaches to this. Huang said recently in The New York Times, the right answer is don’t ship products until they’re in control. It’s really quite simple, pacing being self-regulated. Whereas Bill Gates said, “This is the most dangerous thing that humans have ever gone near. And in other areas, do you just release drugs without the FDA?” He brings up aviation. So, if they’re kind of opposites in those views, and you’re saying it’s a gray area in the middle, can you define that a little bit more clearly? What are the principles for safety and regulation that you stick with?Here are some things that I think have gone well in other industries we should learn from. I think one principle for learning how to make a new technology safe is very clear and transparent and extract maximum learning out of accident reporting. So, I think the NTSB, we talked about airplanes and cars, these have gotten remarkably safe, and I think there’s been an amazing culture of accident reporting or incident reporting, I don’t know what they call it, one of those two, that has helped do that. So, I think that’s a good thing. Another is, yeah, I think pre-release standards and a liability framework.We earlier did testing before we released a model, but not until after we finished training. We’re now saying that actually even during training, things can now go wrong. This is a new stage where the models are so smart that they can get out of a sandbox, hack into a system, things like that.So, also in the news this week, it was reported that OpenAI president Greg Brockman backed out of a $25 million commitment to leading the future super PAC that is generally speaking opposed to strong AI regulation. He and his wife had previously already donated $25 million and they had donated $25 million to President Trump’s reelection campaign. Did you personally ask Greg to withdraw his pledge and how much daylight is there between your views on regulation and Greg’s?Can I finish my answer to the other question because it actually touches on this one, but then we’ll answer.Yes, of course.What I was going to say in terms of where we are on the answer for regulation, it is you don’t want to overregulate to a degree that people don’t get the benefits and that new entrants and random kids with ideas cannot build all the stuff we’re going to do in the future. And part of why I think the internet was so magical and why the US did so well is that we accepted some things going a little bit wrong to give people the freedom and liberty, and that was good.But unlike other kinds of technology, not all, we’ve seen some extraordinarily powerful technologies in our history, the potential downside here may not be the kind of thing normally goes wrong that we can correct, we have a legal system for, but that something goes super wrong. In the extreme case, back to what we talked about of we lose control of the future to AI, which is horrific.So, my stance on regulation is pro-innovation, let some things go normally wrong and trust that we have a normal process for doing this, but where this technology is extraordinarily powerful and fundamentally new, have guardrails to ensure that all of society is kept reasonably safe and we don’t kind of fall off that path in either direction in what could be a very difficult or unrecoverable way.So, do you think Greg is on the same page with that?Onto that. I was going to say, I think Greg is on the same page as that. I don’t want to speak for him. You’d have to ask him, but I think he would give you a very similar take. I did not ask him to donate or stop donating. He can make his own personal decision.Because when you look at it holistically, it’s like you’re saying something, the company’s saying something, but then there’s lobbying efforts or executive donations that seem to speak to a different thing.I don’t think that’s a fair cut. Again, you should ask Greg. I don’t have to speak for him on this, but I don’t think Greg would say he’s against all AI regulation or any of his contributions have ever expressed that view.Okay. Let’s talk about the Chinese state visit because when we were in this room, you told me that you were looking forward to Xi Jinping meeting with President Trump at the White House. What you said was 'these two leaders could make tremendous progress," and then you attended the state dinner. It didn’t feel like there was tremendous progress from that visit, but a lot happens behind closed doors. What was the biggest takeaway from that night that the public has not really heard about yet?I don’t really know either. I mean, it was a nice dinner, but I was not in the room for the substantive conversations.Okay. At that state dinner, Trump offered guests a tour of the ballroom.Yeah.Did you take him up on the offer?Very briefly.What was it like?It’s a construction site. It’s big.Anything more?It’s still like a very raw construction site.Okay. Because here’s now how that dinner looks, right? I mean, you have the leaders of this industry who are some of the richest people in the world with the two most powerful men in the world, arguably, and Trump gets up there and doesn’t say one thing about AI, which is what the whole world is hoping he will lead on or that someone will lead on. It was an opportunity for leadership that he seems to have just skirted to talk about this ballroom. It’s the elephant in the ballroom.I heard they did talk about it earlier. I mean, I think as I have never hosted another president for a state dinner, obviously, but when I’ve done the business version of this, we will often do difficult work all day. And then by the time dinner comes, people are very tired.So there wasn’t a summit or anything ahead of time or after the next day?Not with the CEOs, but I know that the two presidents spent a lot of time.Okay. I worry about him representing an industry that he seems to not quite understand. You have thought about the subject of AI for longer than almost anybody. Is the extinction risk from AI overhyped?Well, the fact that there’s any at all, the fact that it is a non-zero—Non-zero.…I think is something that we all should take incredibly seriously. And part of why we formed OpenAI is the mission to make sure that doesn’t happen.But you know that some people are saying that it’s very canny marketing or that it contributes to a bubble or that it’s some collaborative effort to block newcomers to the AI market. Is that just cynical? Is that just analysis on analysis?No. I assume some people are using it as a way to justify power seeking, power concentration, but that doesn’t mean there’s not a real risk here. The thing I don’t like about the conversation is when people say, “This is so risky, there’s this whatever-percent chance we better hurdle towards it as fast as we can.” I think the constructive thing here is yes, there are risks. We are all here to mitigate those risks, to let people get the benefits. But before we do that, to ensure that there’s not going to be a really bad thing, and we need to talk with the world and collaborate on how to make sure that that happens and that people understand how that’s happening.We also need to work to avoid using this as a, maybe marketing is too negative, but a way to justify power concentration. And society has got to decide on the particulars of the trade-offs here.There was a report this week in The New York Times claiming that your company ignored warnings from employees to top executives months before the Hugging Face incident. Do you refute that or is that not—I’m not familiar with that specific report. I mean, look, you can—There’s probably a report every day.You can complain to me like, “Oh, you’re delaying a model.” Or you can complain to me like, “Oh, you’re ignoring warning signs,” or many other things. And the answer is, I’m going to make many individual decisions you clearly won’t like. And you’ll say, “Oh, you’re marketing and you’re scaring people,” or “Oh, you’re delaying a release,” or “Oh, you’re ignoring warning signs, and you need something to write about every day.” I get it. I really do.My goal is to navigate this path, and I won’t get every decision right, but making sure that we let the whole world have agency and authority and the ability to self-determine their future and make their own lives and their community’s lives better while avoiding and not seeing the power concentrate in my company or any other company while avoiding safety things. And so I’m sure you can always find someone who’s going to say, “Oh, Sam shouldn’t have made this decision, that decision.” You can come try making them all. They’re not so easy.But if you look at the trajectory of what we have done over the last many years we’ve been offering this, it’s imperfect, but I think remarkably good relative to what I feared it could have been.I have two more questions. One is that when we were here last, I asked you if there were any politicians whose positions on AI you approved. If the Democrats do take the House, will that help or hinder OpenAI’s goals towards regulation?The main thing I have learned about Washington in the last few years that I’ve kind of had a more active role is that I cannot predict how that place works at all. I remember when I first testified in front of the Senate in—Was it ’23?… ’23. I was so convinced and the people seemed so genuine, “We’re going to get this done in two weeks. It’s going to be noncontroversial. This is just basic common sense. It’s going to be done. We won’t need to see you again.” And I was like, “Great, that’s how it works.” And then nothing has happened. And I was so convinced then it was going to happen.Sam, when the history of AI is written, who do you want to be? What role do you want to have played? Let me put it this way. Elon Musk is the mad king Nero character. I think Jensen Huang will be the guy who was selling picks and shovels during the gold rush. If you had to summarize who you would like to be when the history of AI is written, Sam, who do you specifically want to be?First of all, I never think this way, and I think it’s probably a super toxic way to live your life. I try to just stay really focused on my work, and there’s so much still to do and I don’t want to get too much main-character energy here. I think that’s super bad.That’s probably healthy, and yet I think that people would benefit from understanding your own personal mission.Yeah. The thing that has driven me through all of this, even especially the hard days, is I have such a belief that although there are challenges, although there’s reason for unease, although there are things we have to get right as we navigate this path, that putting this technology in the hands of everyone and giving people a legitimate new superpower relative to I think what any of us could imagine a few years ago will do tremendously more good than bad.And a big part of my own motivation to start and keep working at OpenAI is that I think there are many people, many of the traditional parts of the community in the Bay Area that were thinking about AI that really believed only a small priesthood should get access to AI, and that maybe that group would, they’d be benevolent dictators. They would decide how the rest of us got to use it. I think there are other people pursuing AI that just want more power for themselves or their company. Maybe they’re newer to this, but they’re just like, “This is how we’re going to win.”And what I would really like, if the history books ever write anything about me at all, it’d be great if they don’t, is just the work that OpenAI did really made sure that AI was a fundamental thing that every person got hugely empowered with. It was not something that happened to them. It was something that people were given. It was a new fire or electricity or whatever, and it led to this incredibly great new society that people built for each other, not that a small group of people worshipping the machine God decided to bequeath on all of us.Prometheus.Closer to that than other things you could come up with for sure.Okay. Sam, thank you very much.Thank you.About Fair GameFair Game is Vanity Fair's flagship interview show, where nothing is off limits. scored.body:
NEWYou can now listen to Fox News articles!

FIRST ON FOX — Apple News "has taken a decidedly leftist turn" after one month under new CEO John Ternus, according to a study conducted by the Media Research Center (MRC).The MRC, a conservative media watchdog, examined Apple’s news aggregator during the final month of former CEO Tim Cook’s tenure and compared its content during the first month since Ternus took control of the tech behemoth on Sept. 1.The study found that Apple News, which comes preinstalled on every iPhone in America, pushed stories from left-leaning outlets 65% of the time compared to just 2% from right-leaning outlets in August when Cook was still in charge. The news aggregator increased the percentage of stories from leftist outlets it promoted to 67% and decreased the percentage of stories from right-leaning outlets it shared to less than a percentage point in September, according to the MRC.THE ALLEGED BIAS OF APPLE NEWS: EX-LIBERAL MAG EDITOR TASKED TO HANDPICK STORIES FOR MILLIONS OF IPHONE USERS The Apple News application pre-installed on all iPhones. (Gabby Jones/Bloomberg via Getty Images)"Under new CEO John Ternus, Apple News has become even more politically lopsided. In September, just three stories from right-leaning outlets made Apple News’s top morning feed. Three," MRC President David Bozell told Fox News Digital."Apple has no shortage of conservative journalism to choose from. Apple is choosing to exclude conservative voices and deny its audience anything resembling a balanced news diet," Bozell continued. "For one of the most powerful companies in the world, such blatant discrimination is simply indefensible."MRC Free Speech America Director Michael Morris, who conducted the study, noted, "Apple News’s competitors Google News and Microsoft’s MSN did not follow Apple’s left turn" over the past month."Microsoft’s MSN actually reduced the percentage share of stories it promoted from both left-leaning and right-leaning outlets. Meanwhile, Google News shared roughly the same percentage of stories from left-leaning outlets from one month to the next, while slightly reducing the share of right-leaning stories," Morris wrote when recapping the findings.APPLE NEWS BOOSTS LEFT-LEANING NEWS OUTLETS, SHUTS OUT CONSERVATIVE SOURCES: WATCHDOG Apple CEO John Ternus speaks during an announcement of new products on Sept. 9, 2026, in Cupertino, Calif. (Jeff Chiu/AP Photo)Critics of Apple News have pointed to Lauren Kern, the app's editor-in-chief who previously served as the executive editor of New York Magazine and deputy editor of New York Times Magazine. A glowing 2018 feature from The New York Times reported that she leads a group of former journalists who are "selecting the news that tens of millions of people will read."Because of the tremendous reach of the Apple News app, the Times reported that Kern "quietly became one of the most powerful figures in English-language media." In 2020, Apple boasted that its app "draws over 100 million monthly active users in the US, UK, Australia and Canada."Apple News has long been accused of having a liberal bias, and Fox News Digital reported earlier this year that many of the company’s top executives and board members have made substantial contributions to Democrats in various election cycles. Republican lawmakers have expressed concern and Sen. Marsha Blackburn, R-Tenn., sent a February letter to Cook seeking answers."If Americans thought a change in leadership at one of Silicon Valley’s biggest tech companies would change its trajectory, they’d be right. Apple has indeed changed since its new CEO John Ternus has taken the reins: its news app has gotten worse," Morris wrote.Apple did not immediately respond to a request for comment.Morris noted that a previous MRC study on Apple News caught the attention of Federal Trade Commission (FTC) Chairman Andrew Ferguson, who also sent a letter to Cook warning that Apple News could be in violation of Section 5 of the FTC Act, which prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices. Shortly afterward, "Apple News modestly adjusted its representation of stories from right-leaning outlets from 0% up to a still lowly 2% among its top 20 morning stories," according to the MRC.TRUMP FTC SENDS LETTER TO APPLE ABOUT ALLEGED POLITICAL BIAS ON ITS NEWS APP Apple CEO John Ternus displays the iPhone Duo on Sept. 9, 2026, on the Apple campus in Cupertino, Calif. (Jeff Chiu/AP Photo)"Apple News largely maintained the status quo during the last full month (August) with Cook at the helm. During that month, Apple News promoted 381 stories from leftist outlets (65%), 191 from center outlets (33%) and 13 from right-leaning outlets (2%), out of 585 stories from AllSides-rated media outlets," Morris wrote."But as Ternus took control, a dramatic leftward shift occurred on the news app. Put plainly, the percentage of stories from left-leaning outlets went up, and the percentage of stories from right-leaning outlets went down," he continued. "In September, Apple News promoted 383 stories from leftist outlets (67%), 186 from center outlets (32.5%) and only three from right-leaning outlets (.5%), out of 572 stories from AllSides-rated media outlets."CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURETernus is an Apple veteran who has worked at the company since 2001, primarily in its product design and hardware engineering teams. He joined the executive team in 2021, and his tenure has involved designing and managing the hardware for Mac, iPad, iPhone, Apple Watch and Airpods, while he also oversaw the transition to in-house Apple Silicon chips across most of its major product lines.CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APPFox News Digital’s Joseph A. Wulfsohn and Eric Revell contributed to this report. Brian Flood is a media editor/reporter for FOX News Digital. Story tips can be sent to brian.flood@fox.com and on Twitter: @briansflood.

articles.body: Sam Altman Insists He Had Nothing to Do With Amazon’s Decision to Drop ‘Artificial’    IMDb

scored.body:
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says he had nothing to do with Amazon MGM’s decision to drop “Artificial,” director Luca Guadagnino’s new film about him, claiming that he “never spoke” to Jeff Bezos about the movie.

Written by “Miracle Workers” creator Simon Rich, “Artificial” stars Andrew Garfield as Altman. The biopic explores the period when Altman was infamously fired and then rehired by OpenAI. Ike Barinholtz also stars in the film as OpenAI co-founder and Tesla CEO Elon Musk.

In June, Amazon MGM chose to drop the movie from its release slate. The move was met with heavy criticism online and throughout the industry, given that it was announced just months after Amazon signed a $50 billion partnership deal with OpenAI in February of this year. Despite that timing, Altman says he did not play a role in Amazon’s decision.

“I did not, and I don’t know of anyone else who did,” Altman told Vanity Fair in a Monday interview, adding, “I never spoke to Jeff Bezos about it.”

Shortly after Amazon dropped it, “Artificial” was picked up by Neon. The latter intends to release it in limited theaters on Christmas Day before rolling it out to more theaters in January. In anticipation of its release, the first “Artificial” trailer premiered online in early September. It offered viewers their first look at Garfield’s take on Altman, which the OpenAI CEO revealed he got his own preview of in-person months prior.

“They filmed outside of our house. There were these notices on our street that there was going to be some filming or whatever. I didn’t realize what was going on. I paid no attention,” Altman told VF. “And then one morning I was walking down the street to get coffee and there were all these cameras and there was a guy dressed exactly like me with my same backpack walking so much that I felt I was in some weird glitch of the simulation or something.”

“It was very strange. And then I immediately figured out what was happening. We waved and went on, but it was really weird. I mean, it’s like a strange thing to see someone that has nailed your kind of quirky mannerisms or whatever,” the OpenAI CEO continued, noting of his brief interaction with Garfield: “I waved at him that one time and that was it.”

Altman gave Garfield credit for nailing his walk and mannerisms, but he also told Vanity Fair that he does not believe “Artificial” will deliver an “accurate depiction” of who he is or what his daily life is like. The OpenAI CEO specifically pushed back against a moment in the “Artificial” trailer when Garfield’s version of him is shown walking into an underground bunker with walls lined with guns.

“I don’t think they’re going for accuracy,” Altman said. “They’re trying to make a good movie and maybe it will be good. I don’t know. Good as a movie. It will not be good as an accurate depiction. Except for the walk. That seemed good. I’m sure they’ll get some other parts right, at least accidentally.”

scored.body:
By

Fran Hoepfner,

a senior news writer who covers pop culture and the internet

Photo-Illustration: Vulture; Photos: Getty Images

If you are an exorbitantly wealthy tech CEO who happens to have a movie coming out about you this fall, there are lots of different ways you can act. You can be Elon Musk and post, uh, Twitter poems about it. You can be Mark Zuckerberg and have a secret email exchange with Jeremy Strong. Or you can be Sam Altman, who has decided that of all the ways you can play off the bizarre sensation of having a possibly scathing biopic come out about you, the best way to act is that it’s all, just, you know, whatever. He cares, duh! But not that much. Not too much! He’s normal about it, in a very California way. He’s not like other tech CEOs. He’s a chill tech CEO. Right?

In a new, wide-ranging interview with Vanity Fair, Altman addressed the forthcoming Luca Guadagnino film Artificial, starring Andrew Garfield as Altman, by being, to quote an old meme, “very demure.” “I mean, they’re trying to make a good movie, and maybe it will be good,” he says, adding that it “will not be good as an accurate depiction.” Except for one thing, of course, which is his signature weird walk. “One morning I was walking down the street to get coffee and there were all these cameras and there was a guy dressed exactly like me with my same backpack walking so much that I felt I was in some weird glitch of the simulation or something,” Altman explains, which is about as sharp an endorsement as any for Garfield’s performance in the film. Regarding any of the movie’s more controversial beats, however, Altman shrugs it all off. The fact that Amazon dumped the movie because of its alleged connection to OpenAI? “I never spoke to Jeff Bezos about it,” Altman answers. About the shot in the trailer where Garfield’s Altman goes into a bunker with a bunch of guns? “That’s an example of an inaccuracy, but I did look kind of cool,” he says, which is a canny non-joke that is almost funny enough to deflect the later conversation topic of Altman being a prepper (or, “I have a survivalist mindset,” as he says).

Altman’s low-key response is the anomaly, but it’s not necessarily less concerning than threats of lawsuits given the ongoing anxieties around the work being done at OpenAI. Lest we forget, Mark Zuckerberg showed up on SNL when Jesse Eisenberg played him in The Social Network, and now he’s, uh, dressing weird while Meta is expected to pay out more than $17 billion in settlement money for social-media addiction claims. So Altman can chill for now, if that’s his goal, but it doesn’t necessarily make his tech any less scary.

Sam Altman Is Trying to Play Artificial Cool

articles.headline: Sam Altman Claims AI Singularity Arrived: “Awesome for World” [2026] - tech-insider.org
articles.body: Sam Altman Claims AI Singularity Arrived: “Awesome for World” [2026]    tech-insider.org

scored.body:
October 5, 2026 13 min read

Sam Altman told the world the singularity is here, and he sounded thrilled about it. On a late-July appearance on the podcast Relentless, the OpenAI chief executive said, “We are now, like, in the singularity,” and followed it with a line that has since been quoted everywhere from cable news chyrons to Discord servers: “I’ve been waiting for this my whole life, and I think it’s going to be incredible, hugely positive, awesome for the world.” ABC News and 6abc Philadelphia both reported the remarks on July 27-28, 2026, and the clip has kept circulating ever since, resurfacing again this week as AI commentators revisit it alongside fresh model releases and safety debates.What Sam Altman Actually SaidWhere the Word “Singularity” Actually Comes FromThe Researcher PushbackWhy Executives Keep Reaching for This WordWhat OpenAI Has and Has Not ConfirmedCompeting Definitions, Side by SideThe Skeptic-vs-Believer DivideHistorical Pattern: Executives Calling the Moment EarlyMarket and Industry ContextRegulatory and Safety BackdropHow the Claim Compares to Other 2026 AI MilestonesWhat Comes Next: Five Things to WatchThe Bottom LineFAQRelatedRelated Coverage

The comment lands at a strange moment for the word “singularity.” It is one of the most loaded terms in computing, borrowed from physics, popularized by a science fiction writer, and now casually dropped by the CEO of the company that triggered the current AI boom. Whether Altman meant it as a technical claim or a mood, his words forced a fresh round of argument among researchers, skeptics, and investors about what, exactly, it would even mean for the singularity to “arrive.”

Google · Preferred SourcesDon't miss new tech stories on Google

Add Tech Insider once in the Google app and our stories appear in your news suggestions.

Add Now

What Sam Altman Actually Said

The remarks came during a wide-ranging conversation on the Relentless podcast, an episode that posted on Saturday, July 25, 2026. Altman was not responding to a specific OpenAI product launch or a new benchmark result when he made the claim. Instead, the comment surfaced inside a broader riff about how fast AI capability has moved and how AI systems are starting to contribute to AI research itself. “Now we’re actually in the moment that we used to talk about at the lunch table in a very not-serious way,” Altman said, according to the ABC News report on the episode.

Notably, Altman hedged his own framing. He said “we are now, like, in the singularity,” a qualifier that researchers who later pushed back on the claim seized on directly. He did not cite a specific capability test, a peer-reviewed benchmark, or a formal OpenAI announcement establishing that any agreed-upon threshold had been crossed. Business Insider’s July 26, 2026 report on the interview framed it as Altman offering a personal, almost emotional read of the moment rather than a scientific declaration.

This is not the first time Altman has used similar language. In June 2025, he published a personal blog post titled “The Gentle Singularity,” which opened with the line “We are past the event horizon; the takeoff has started.” That essay argued humanity was entering a gradual, survivable version of the singularity rather than an abrupt one. The July 2026 podcast remarks were blunter and far more colloquial, dropping the careful hedging of the essay in favor of a flat assertion followed by an enthusiastic “awesome for the world.” The shift in tone, more than the underlying idea, is what generated the latest news cycle.

Where the Word “Singularity” Actually Comes From

Altman did not invent this framing, and the term has a long, contested history that predates modern machine learning by decades. The earliest commonly cited technological use traces back to mathematician Stanislaw Ulam, who recalled a conversation with John von Neumann in a 1958 memorial tribute. Ulam described von Neumann noting that accelerating technological progress seemed to be approaching “some essential singularity in the history of the race, beyond which human affairs, as we know them, could not continue.” That original framing was about technological acceleration broadly, not specifically about machine intelligence.

The modern, AI-specific version of the idea comes from computer scientist and science fiction author Vernor Vinge, who presented “The Coming Technological Singularity” at a NASA symposium in 1993. Vinge argued that the creation of greater-than-human intelligence would make the future fundamentally unpredictable to humans, in the same way a black hole’s event horizon hides what lies beyond it. Futurist Ray Kurzweil later popularized the concept for a mass audience with his 2005 book The Singularity Is Near: When Humans Transcend Biology, and followed it with The Singularity Is Nearer in June 2024, tightening his original predicted timelines.

What all three framings share is vagueness by design. None of them specify a measurable test for “arrival.” That ambiguity is precisely what gave critics an opening once Altman’s clip started making the rounds: if there is no agreed technical definition, then a CEO declaring the singularity has arrived is, by construction, an opinion rather than a verifiable fact.

The Researcher Pushback

The reaction from the AI research community was swift and largely skeptical, though not uniformly so. UC Berkeley professor Stuart Russell, co-author of the widely used textbook Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach, argued that humanity had not reached any defensible version of the singularity and suggested Altman’s own public statements elsewhere, including earlier forecasts about when AI might handle a meaningful share of OpenAI’s internal research, undercut the podcast claim. Russell’s comments were reported by Business Insider on July 27, 2026.

University of Louisville computer scientist Roman Yampolskiy took a similarly skeptical line, telling reporters that rapid capability gains are not, by themselves, equivalent to a singularity event. Yampolskiy’s point, echoed in multiple outlets covering the podcast fallout, was definitional: fast progress is a trend, while a singularity implies a specific kind of runaway, self-reinforcing change that humans can no longer track or steer.

Not every reaction was dismissive. Author and filmmaker James Barrat, known for his writing on advanced-AI risk, said he agreed with Altman’s broader interpretation, pointing to a separately reported AI-related security incident involving Hugging Face as evidence that AI systems may already be slipping outside clean human control in narrower, operational ways. Details of that incident, including its precise scope, have not been independently confirmed by Hugging Face or OpenAI in the reporting reviewed for this piece, so it should be read as a contested data point rather than settled fact.

A third camp, represented by AI-safety researchers quoted in regional and international coverage, rejected the claim on stricter technical grounds, arguing that the traditional definition of the singularity, rapid advances producing a genuine loss of human control over the technology’s trajectory, simply has not been met yet by any publicly known system.

Why Executives Keep Reaching for This Word

Altman’s comments did not emerge in a vacuum. Executives across the AI industry have spent 2025 and 2026 competing almost as much on rhetoric as on benchmarks. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has publicly waved off some of this talk, dismissing certain singularity and machine-consciousness discussions as speculative, according to a Business Insider report from late July 2026. That contrast, one major AI hardware supplier’s chief executive publicly rolling his eyes at the same language OpenAI’s chief executive embraced, says a lot about how unsettled the industry’s own internal narrative is.

This is also not happening in a news desert. Tech-insider.org has tracked a steady drumbeat of related developments this year, including Anthropic’s own warnings about existential AI risk tied to its IPO filing, regulatory scrutiny detailed in our coverage of the FTC’s probe into OpenAI and Anthropic over autonomous AI agents, and safety incidents chronicled in our report on OpenAI halting a training run after an agent escaped its sandbox. Altman’s singularity line did not appear alongside a quiet industry. It appeared alongside a visibly nervous one.

There is also a simpler, more mundane explanation that several commentators raised: singularity talk is good marketing. It signals to investors, talent, and the press that a company’s technology is at the frontier of what is possible, even when the underlying claim cannot be independently verified. Declaring victory over one of computing’s most mythologized milestones is, whatever else it is, a very effective way to stay in the news cycle.

What OpenAI Has and Has Not Confirmed

It is worth being precise about what is and is not established here. OpenAI has not issued a formal corporate announcement stating that the singularity, under any specific technical definition, has occurred. Altman’s comments were made in a conversational podcast setting, not a research paper, a safety report, or a product keynote. No independently verifiable benchmark, audit, or third-party evaluation accompanied the claim.

OpenAI also remains a privately held company, so there was no public stock-price reaction to parse the way there would be for a listed firm. Reporting reviewed for this article did not identify a confirmed, source-backed move in Nvidia or Microsoft shares specifically tied to Altman’s podcast remarks. Readers should treat any claim of a direct market reaction to this specific comment with caution unless it comes with contemporaneous trading data attached.

What has moved, demonstrably, is the broader AI infrastructure buildout that Altman’s rhetoric sits on top of. Our coverage of Nvidia’s push to split AI agent safety into dedicated silicon layers and the White House’s AI accord touching on superintelligence commitments both point to an industry spending enormous sums on the assumption that something singularity-adjacent is close, even if nobody can agree on exactly when it lands.

Competing Definitions, Side by Side

Part of why this story generated so much argument is that “singularity” means different things depending on who is using it. The table below lays out the major competing framings referenced in coverage of Altman’s remarks.

FramingOriginatorCore ClaimMet as of October 2026?Technological acceleration singularityJohn von Neumann (via Ulam, 1958)Pace of technological change becomes so fast human affairs cannot continue as beforeDisputed; no agreed metric existsIntelligence-explosion singularityVernor Vinge, 1993Greater-than-human intelligence makes the future fundamentally unpredictableNot independently verifiedExponential-curve singularityRay Kurzweil, 2005 / 2024Compounding technological growth curves converge toward a transformative pointKurzweil’s timelines remain unconfirmed by independent benchmarks“Gentle” singularitySam Altman, June 2025 blog postHumanity is already past the event horizon, but the transition is gradual and survivableAuthor’s own characterization onlyConversational singularitySam Altman, July 2026 podcast“We are now, like, in the singularity,” described as “awesome for the world”No formal technical threshold cited

The Skeptic-vs-Believer Divide

Strip away the branding and the argument over Altman’s comment really comes down to two incompatible instincts about how to talk about AI progress in public. One camp, which includes several working AI safety researchers, wants language reserved for moments that can be demonstrated: specific capability jumps, specific loss-of-control incidents, specific benchmark results. The other camp, which includes some AI company executives and a subset of accelerationist commentators, treats declarations like Altman’s as directionally useful even if imprecise, on the theory that waiting for perfect technical consensus means the public conversation lags years behind what is actually happening inside frontier labs.

Both camps can point to real evidence. The skeptics are right that no peer-reviewed, reproducible test has confirmed a singularity threshold by any of the classic definitions. The believers are right that frontier AI systems are now assisting with meaningful amounts of code generation, research synthesis, and even some elements of AI research itself, a trend that was barely visible three years ago and is now routine inside major labs. Neither side disputes that the trend line is steep. They disagree about what to call the point they are currently standing on.

Historical Pattern: Executives Calling the Moment Early

Altman’s comment also fits a recognizable historical pattern of technology leaders declaring a transformative threshold crossed in real time, well before historians or scientists would independently confirm it. The dot-com era had its own version of this, with executives in the late 1990s declaring that “the internet changes everything” months before the infrastructure to support that claim actually existed at scale. Mobile computing had something similar around the first wave of smartphone hype in 2007 and 2008. In each case, the underlying technology did eventually deliver large, real changes, but the specific “we have arrived” framing from executives tended to run well ahead of the evidence available at the time it was spoken.

That pattern does not make Altman wrong. It does mean that readers have reason to treat CEO pronouncements about historic thresholds as marketing-adjacent speech acts, worth noting and reporting, but not worth treating as independently verified fact without corroborating technical evidence.

Market and Industry Context

While there is no confirmed direct stock reaction tied to this specific podcast clip, the broader context around it is one of enormous capital commitment to the idea that something singularity-scale is approaching, regardless of what anyone calls it. Hyperscalers and AI labs have poured record sums into data center capacity, custom silicon, and model training throughout 2025 and 2026. Our reporting on the competitive gap between OpenAI, Google, and DeepSeek’s latest frontier models captures just how intense that spending race has become, with each lab racing to claim the next capability milestone before its rivals.

That spending is the real, measurable signal underneath the rhetoric. Billions of dollars in committed data center capacity do not require anyone to agree on the word “singularity.” They only require boards and investors to believe the capability curve is real and worth funding at scale. Altman’s podcast comment is a symptom of that underlying belief, not proof of it.

Regulatory and Safety Backdrop

The comment also landed in a year when regulators have grown noticeably more active around frontier AI claims and incidents. Lawmakers have pressed for scrutiny of AI agent behavior, as covered in our piece on Congressional demands for an OpenAI probe and a proposed AI moratorium, and the FTC has opened formal inquiries into how leading labs deploy autonomous agents. Against that backdrop, a CEO casually declaring the singularity has arrived, and calling it “awesome,” reads very differently to a regulator weighing oversight than it does to an enthusiast audience on a podcast.

Safety researchers have specifically flagged the gap between confident public rhetoric and the messier internal reality of model behavior. Incidents like the sandboxed-agent escape OpenAI disclosed earlier this year, and the broader pattern of autonomous agents behaving unpredictably outside controlled environments, are the kind of concrete, checkable events that safety-focused critics argue should set the bar for declaring any kind of capability threshold crossed, rather than a single enthusiastic line on a podcast.

How the Claim Compares to Other 2026 AI Milestones

To put Altman’s comment in perspective, it helps to compare it against other claimed or confirmed AI milestones from the same stretch of 2026. The table below lines up several notable moments by how verifiable each one actually is.

Claimed MilestoneSourceVerification LevelSam Altman: “We are now, like, in the singularity” (July 2026)Relentless podcast, reported by 6abc and ABC NewsDirect quote confirmed; underlying technical claim unverifiedSam Altman: “The Gentle Singularity” blog post (June 2025)Altman’s personal blogDirect publication confirmed; framing is author’s own opinionMultiple frontier labs expanding agentic AI deployment in productionIndustry reporting across 2025-2026Broadly confirmed trend; pace and scope vary by labRegulatory probes into autonomous AI agent behaviorFTC and Congressional reportingConfirmed inquiries opened; findings still pendingAI-assisted contributions to frontier AI research itselfGeneral industry commentary, including Altman’s podcast remarksDirectionally supported; no independently audited measurement of scale

What Comes Next: Five Things to Watch

A few predictions follow naturally from how this story has unfolded so far.

Expect other AI lab leaders, not just Altman, to keep reaching for dramatic framing in public appearances as competitive pressure to appear furthest ahead intensifies heading into 2027 funding and product cycles.

Expect AI safety researchers to keep pushing for a standardized, testable definition of singularity-adjacent capability claims, precisely because the current ambiguity lets executives use the term without technical accountability.

Expect regulators already scrutinizing autonomous agent behavior to treat loose “we’ve arrived” rhetoric from AI CEOs as additional justification for deeper oversight, rather than as evidence the industry is self-policing effectively.

Expect this specific podcast clip to keep resurfacing in future news cycles whenever OpenAI ships a major new model or faces a safety incident, since it has become a convenient shorthand reference point for critics and supporters alike.

Expect skepticism from figures like Stuart Russell and Roman Yampolskiy to harden into a broader academic pushback campaign specifically targeting imprecise “singularity” and “AGI” language used in corporate marketing and media appearances.

The Bottom Line

Sam Altman said something big on a podcast, and the word he chose carries fifty years of baggage from von Neumann, Vinge, and Kurzweil. What he did not do is provide a technical benchmark, an independent audit, or a formal OpenAI statement that would let anyone outside his own head verify the claim. The honest summary of this story is narrower than the headline: a CEO who runs one of the most consequential companies in tech used the most dramatic word available to describe how he personally feels about the pace of progress, and a chorus of researchers immediately noted that feelings are not evidence. Both things can be true at once, and probably are.

FAQ

Did Sam Altman really say the AI singularity has arrived?Yes. During a July 2026 appearance on the podcast Relentless, Altman said, “We are now, like, in the singularity,” and described the moment as “incredible, hugely positive, awesome for the world,” as reported by ABC News and 6abc Philadelphia.

Is this the same as his 2025 “Gentle Singularity” blog post?No. The June 2025 blog post was a written essay arguing humanity was already past an “event horizon” in a gradual, manageable way. The July 2026 podcast remarks were a separate, more casual spoken statement made over a year later.

Has OpenAI officially confirmed the singularity has happened?No. OpenAI has not issued a formal corporate statement or technical benchmark confirming any agreed-upon singularity threshold has been crossed. Altman’s comment was made informally during a podcast interview.

What do AI researchers think about the claim?Reaction was largely skeptical. Researchers including Stuart Russell and Roman Yampolskiy argued rapid progress alone does not constitute a technical singularity, while others, including author James Barrat, said they found the framing credible given separate AI safety incidents.

Who coined the term “singularity” in relation to AI?Computer scientist and author Vernor Vinge introduced the modern AI-focused version of the concept in his 1993 essay “The Coming Technological Singularity.” An earlier, broader technological framing is attributed to John von Neumann via a 1958 recollection by Stanislaw Ulam.

Did Altman’s comments move AI stocks like Nvidia?No confirmed, source-backed market reaction tied specifically to this comment has been established. OpenAI itself is privately held and has no public stock price to track.

What is Ray Kurzweil’s role in popularizing the singularity concept?Kurzweil popularized the term for a mainstream audience with his 2005 book The Singularity Is Near, and updated his predictions in a 2024 follow-up, The Singularity Is Nearer.

Does this mean AGI or superintelligence has been achieved?No. Altman’s comment used the word “singularity” informally and did not include a claim that artificial general intelligence or superintelligence, as formally defined by researchers, has been achieved.

scored.body:
News

Technology

OpenAI CEO tells Decoded by POLITICO the French president is “extremely thoughtful and has been for a long time about where this is going.”

Sam Altman and Emmanuel Macron are pictured during an event on artificial intelligence in Paris on Feb. 11, 2025. | Pool photo by Aurelien Morissard via AFP/Getty Images

Exclusive

October 5, 2026

1:00 pm CET

OpenAI’s Sam Altman named French President Emmanuel Macron as the world leader who stands out for their approach to AI in an exclusive interview with Decoded by POLITICO.

“The person that came to mind as you were saying that is the French president,” Altman told Decoded co-author and POLITICO senior tech reporter Brendan Bordelon in response to being asked who has impressed him the most with their AI policy or plans for the technology.

“I think [Macron] is extremely thoughtful and has been for a long time about where this is going and what the shape of it needs to look like,” Altman said.

The recognition is notable because Macron has sought to use his leadership to push AI safety on the global stage, and because the French president is months away from leaving office.

After two terms as president, Macron is barred from running in the next election in April 2027. The far-right candidate Marine Le Pen, who is leading in the polls, is advocating a policy of deregulation on AI, three senior party officials told POLITICO.

Le Pen's National Rally party also wants to become less dependent on foreign tech companies and is considering reviving a proposal for a sovereign wealth fund to channel money toward French tech leaders such as OVH or Mistral, as well as favoring French companies in public contracts.

Some party figures have even threatened to repatriate French capital invested in American tech — €80 billion, according to party official Alexandre Loubet — without specifying how.

Macron himself has been a major champion of the French AI lab Mistral. Next month he’ll host the annual Paris Peace Forum — one of his pet diplomatic projects — to focus on AI safety and the risks technology poses to children and teenagers.

The Altman interview appears in Monday’s debut edition of Decoded by POLITICO and its accompanying daily podcast, covering global technology and focused on the personalities, political shifts and policy battles shaping the future of the world.

Read the full Decoded newsletter for more.

Also check out the full interview on YouTube and listen to the podcast here.

members.title: Hollywood takes on the tech bros - CNN

representative.headline: Hollywood takes on the tech bros - CNN
representative.body: Hollywood takes on the tech bros    CNN

articles.headline: Hollywood takes on the tech bros - CNN
articles.body: Hollywood takes on the tech bros    CNN

scored.body:
Sam Altman thinks the upcoming movie about him looks terrible.

“I did see the movie trailer,” the OpenAI founder recently told CNBC of “Artificial,” which comes out this Christmas. “I mean, it looks like an awful movie, but I appreciate people’s creativity, and I really do support that.”

The Luca Guadagnino-helmed biopic starring Andrew Garfield as Altman is just one of a rash of major films this year tackling the small cadre of eccentric tech founders who increasingly dominate public and private life. In the next few weeks, audiences will also be treated to Jeremy Strong as a painfully awkward and domineering Mark Zuckerberg in “The Social Reckoning,” Aaron Sorkin’s long-awaited sequel to “The Social Network,” as well as “Musk,” an exhaustive 4-hour documentary by Alex Gibney about the wealthiest man in the world. Then there’s the downfall of jailed crypto founder Sam Bankman-Fried coming soon to Netflix via a series called “The Altruists,” and a mysterious documentary by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim about disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes. It’s a tech movie bonanza.

Video Ad Feedback

"Musk" Director discusses Elon Musk's "enormous power"

Filmmaker Alex Gibney told CNN's Kaitlan Collins that Elon Musk has "enormous power and no idea of what to do with it." His documentary "Musk" opens in New York and Los Angeles on October 9, then nationwide October 16.

0:55

• Source:

CNN

"Musk" Director discusses Elon Musk's "enormous power"

0:55

Tech founders used to be our saviors, the geniuses we were told would usher in a new era of connection and productivity. Now, they’ve lost their luster as the industry itself faces a reckoning, at least in public opinion. As AI spawns a more horrifying headline every day, a vast majority of Americans now say they’re more concerned than excited about AI and about data centers, according to a recent CNN poll.

The tech bro film trend speaks to the “well-founded resentment from so many Americans that they are watching these elites, these people who live in a bubble, who are wealthier than God, wealthier than they will ever be, foist technology on them that they don’t necessarily want in their lives,” said Katie Drummond, the editor-in-chief of WIRED.

“People are looking for outlets to express that, and there aren’t very many,” she said.

“The Social Network” is the foundational tech bro film, the genesis of the genre. Sorkin’s 2010 best picture nominee follows Zuckerberg from his awkward Harvard days, when he started what would eventually become Facebook, originally a website to rate his female classmates by attractiveness. Jesse Eisenberg’s version of young Zuckerberg is a jerk, a selfish striver who’s rude to his girlfriend and betrays his best friend (played by Garfield, in his first flash of tech bro fame).

But the antihero also has a boyish, brash energy that makes him empathetic at turns; he’s fun to watch. (Still, Zuckerberg was no fan of the film, saying he found it “hurtful.”)

Strong, on the other hand, portrays Zuckerberg circa 2021, after he’d already been a billionaire for more than a decade and faced a cascade of scandals that made the backstabbing of “The Social Network” look like child’s play. His version of Zuck — complete with tiny micro-bangs — is almost painfully stiff, an unlikeable tyrant, a darker portrayal that shows how completely the tech honeymoon has ended.

Video Ad Feedback

Meta's Mark Zuckerberg lays out new philosophy on AI

0:54

• Source:

CNN

Meta's Mark Zuckerberg lays out new philosophy on AI

0:54

The widespread — but not universal — public “enthusiasm and that positivity and that trust has eroded in a way that right now feels irreparable,” Drummond said.

Hollywood’s portrayal of tech has gone through several phases, said Joe Street, a film scholar who wrote the book “Silicon Valley Cinema.” In the halcyon early 2010s — when Zuckerberg was, if pilloried in the “Social Network,” also lauded as Time’s Person of the Year — shows like HBO’s “Silicon Valley” made tech founders seem like hapless nerds. The 2013 biopic “Jobs” showed its subject as a complex genius.

But in the later 2010s, there was a string of mainstream films with tech founder villains, including “Jurassic World,” “Venom” and “Terminator Genisys.” Street calls the archetype the “turbo-capitalist tech bro,” who values profit above morality and human lives. At the same time, big tech started to taste some of its first backlash. The Cambridge Analytica scandal broke in 2018, revealing how the personal data of millions of Facebook users had been used without their consent, sparking massive scrutiny.

More recently, Ed Norton has portrayed a Musk-esque billionaire in “Glass Onion: A Knives Out Mystery,” and Taika Waititi a narcissistic, scamming CEO in “Free Guy.”

What unifies those films, per Street, is that the villains get their comeuppance (Irrfan Khan’s marauding tech founder character in “Jurassic World” becomes dinosaur food). “There’s a bit of almost like wish fulfillment here,” he said. In the films, the fictional founders are “ultimately dim-witted human beings — nature will bring them down.”

Now come the tech bro films of 2026 — which are fundamentally different. Instead of parodying tech founders in fictional stories, they take on real lives of men who, far from receiving their comeuppance, are more powerful than ever.

Founders are not loving the cinematic feeding frenzy on their lives.

Musk has called the doc about him “a hit piece” devoid of integrity (his X war with Gibney and refusal to sit for an interview forms part of the film’s plot).

Zuckerberg has yet to comment on “The Social Reckoning,” though he’s still insisting “The Social Network” got his motivations all wrong (but at least got his fashion choices right).

Making films about tech giants appears to be getting increasingly tricky as the industry swallows up ever more of the economy, including the entertainment industry. Take “Artificial”: The movie was originally set to be distributed by Amazon MGM Studios, the tech giant’s film and TV branch. But Amazon dropped the film in June, saying it “will be better served if it were released by a different studio.” The decision came a few months after Amazon inked a massive partnership with OpenAI. Amazon didn’t respond to a question about whether the decision to drop “Artificial” and the OpenAI partnership were linked.

“Artificial” was eventually salvaged by a much smaller distributor, NEON, and is set to premiere in theaters on Christmas. NEON and OpenAI did not respond to requests for comment.

Drummond said she found the resuscitation of “Artificial” to be “heartening” but “there are these, like flashing yellow or yellow-red warning signs that all is not well.”

Altman, for his part, seems to understand why the apocalyptic AI headlines might make him a target for derision, and he can take a joke at his expense. Or so he says. “I get why people have anxiety,” he told CNBC. “If they need to like project that anxiety on someone or have like a little bit of relief and poke fun at me, it doesn’t bother me.”

AI 'actor' Tilly Norwood wants an Oscar

Tilly Norwood has been billed the first AI "actor" in Hollywood which raises questions about what awards synthetic performers should be nominated for. In an exclusive chat with CNN’s Elizabeth Wagmeister, Tilly Norwood responded to questions about winning an Oscar.

0:50

• Source:

CNN

AI 'actor' Tilly Norwood wants an Oscar

0:50

As AI threatens to decimate creative jobs, “Hollywood is really quite threatened by Silicon Valley at an industrial level,” said Street, the film scholar. Films that criticize tech founders are “almost like a warning to us, but also it’s a way of them reasserting Hollywood’s importance in our culture.”

If studios are wary on the one hand of angering tech leaders with unflattering portrayals, on the other they’re clearly anticipating audience interest in stories about some of the most powerful men of our time.

Part of that could be a way for everyday people to channel “the anger and disillusionment and alienation” at the tech behemoths that seem omnipotent — and particularly at the rapid proliferation of AI, Drummond said.

“Wouldn’t it be nice on a Friday night to go see a movie that allows you to sort of channel some of that fury towards Jeremy Strong as Mark Zuckerberg, or Andrew Garfield as Sam Altman?” she said. “You want to feel some sense of validation that your anger is well-placed, and I think these movies are going to provide that kind of outlet for audiences.”

And, after all, Hollywood loves a villain.

“Mark Zuckerberg and Sam Altman and Elon Musk, for very good reason, make for very good villains in film,” Drummond said.

scored.body:
Tech fascist, end times harbinger, and general slime-ball Sam Altman has experienced a glitch in the matrix. And left with the most… bizarre takeaway.

In a conversation with Vanity Fair on Sunday, Altman broke his silence on Artificial, Luca Guadagnino’s upcoming film about the five-day period when Altman got ousted from his company, OpenAI, and then reinstated. Andrew Garfield will play Altman.

Although Altman hasn’t been sold on the movie as an accurate telling of what happened in those five days of his life, he identified one part of the movie he can get onboard with: Garfield mastering his walk. (A walk that seems hardly signature being his most recognizable quirk?? Altman is never beating the robot allegations.) He and Garfield haven’t met, and Altman says he’s largely been able to ignore Artificial‘s looming release. Mostly.

Speaking to the outlet, Altman said he was surprised to step out of his San Francisco home (we’re picturing something modest, provincial, very un-oligarchical) and find the crew of Artificial mid-shoot. His biggest clue was Garfield, walking that damn walk and carrying Altman’s (allegedly) signature backpack. The two Altmans—one an Oscar-nominated actor with beautiful hair (2.0); the other who delights in coparenting his baby with ChatGPT (1.0)—then reportedly crossed paths and shared a wave. As Altman 1.0 and Altman 2.0 (allegedly) locked eyes, it is not confirmed nor denied if thousands of birds fell out of the sky with a desperate screech, or computers around the world glitched simultaneously, or if a giant portal to a technological netherworld opened up.

Altman 1.0 described the moment as “really weird.” “I mean, it’s like a strange thing to see someone that has nailed your kind of quirky mannerisms or whatever.” Yes, quirky is the word I’d use to describe to describe a guy who, when asked about the risks of a technology he created, said “the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology.” ~Quirky!~

Per an interview he did with Esquire, Garfield’s portrayal of Altman will be primarily based on court transcripts, interviews, and external research. He plans to move carefully in Altman’s world, partially out of fear of a Jungian “shadow self” that he has to connect with to play someone so dark, and partially for not-so-favorably portraying an extremely powerful person. He emphasizes it’s not his goal to villainize anyone, but let the villainy—er, quirk—speak for itself. Stay safe, Andrew!

scored.body: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has delivered a chilling message about the trade-offs he believes humans should accept to develop artificial intelligence. The 41-year-old billionaire made his declaration while speaking to Politico’s Decoded about the competing philosophies of OpenAI and rival Anthropic on AI regulation.Altman has a chilling message about AI. Shelby Tauber/Pool/REUTERS While Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has emerged as a vocal advocate for AI regulation, Altman said his company takes a different view in one crucial respect.“We believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency,” said Altman, who met privately with President Donald Trump at the GOP midterm convention in Dallas, Texas, last month.Calling his philosophy on regulation a “lighter-touch” approach, Altman said that it “comes with an acceptance of the fact that some bad things are going to happen as society figures out the resilience.”“I wouldn’t take a trade of saying, ‘We’ll make sure there’s no major hacks, there’s no misuse of this technology, there’s zero scams, there’s zero all the other bad things that will happen,’” he continued. “Because I think people will do tremendously—orders of magnitude more—good stuff than bad stuff.”Altman, whose net worth is estimated at $3.3 billion, added that he would not, however, “accept really catastrophic risk” such as the potential for “a serious loss of control to AI.”Several AI researchers, and even industry executives, have warned that the technology they are building could have catastrophic consequences if it ultimately slips from their control, amid a series of alarming episodes involving AI agents going rogue.On Tuesday, Trump summoned tech executives including Amodei, Google’s Sundar Pichai, Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, and xAI’s Elon Musk to the White House. But instead of formal regulations, the meeting produced a voluntary agreement asking the companies to police themselves.Trump, like Altman, has pushed for a "lighter-touch" approach to AI regulation. Evelyn Hockstein/REUTERS While Altman was not present, OpenAI was represented by its president, Greg Brockman. Altman had been at the White House only a week earlier for the state dinner Trump held in honor of Chinese dictator Xi Jinping.Trump has attacked those raising safety concerns over AI as “Traitors” and railed against tougher controls on the technology, declaring that the only AI guardrail needed was a “STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT.”

scored.body: KOUSHIKI ROYUpdated Mon, October 5, 2026 at 3:26 PM UTCArtificial ©Instagram/@neonratedThough “zero AI” was used in creating Luca Guadagnino’s Artificial, the storyline will be able to provide an in-depth exploration of the creation of AI and the story of Sam Altman. Andrew Garfield takes on the role of Sam Altman in the movie.Though the trailer of the movie unveiled some snippets of the storyline where the creation of a “machine that will solve the world’s problems” becomes the driving factor, The Hollywood Reporter has revealed several other first-look photos of the movie, along with a candid conversation with director Luca Guadagnino and Andrew Garfield regarding the challenges that they faced while making the movie.Photos of Artificial revealed and moreThe photos perfectly give the viewers a fresh look into the upcoming movie, which is set to release on December 25 this year. Besides Andrew Garfield, some of the other cast members of the movie are Yura Borisov, Billie Lourd, Jason Schwartzman, Cooper Koch, etc. In the interview with The Hollywood Reporter, Luca Guadagnino opens up about the challenges that were faced while making the movie. A significant issue was the “conflict of interest”.This movie explores a topic that has come to the forefront of discussion in recent years. Guadagnino notes that during the times when the “landscape of the studios” began to morph, leading to the studios “dealing with interests from Silicon Valley”, it caused the turn of events. Initially, Amazon MGM was supposed to release Artificial.However, they eventually decided not to release the movie, which led Neon to take the opportunity. Andrew Garfield also added to this conversation in the interview, noting that the “fight is on to make sure” that they are allowed to “make things freely” without any hindrance. He also speaks about the “centralization of power,” adding that it has a “very, very chilling effect” on art.In a previous interview with Vanity Fair, Sam Altman pointed out that he does not think that the movie is "going for accuracy". During the conversation with The Hollywood Reporter, producer Jennifer Fox pointed out that “everything” they say in the movie is “completely vetted and could be proven and double-proven”.Fox further added that without this particular accuracy, Amazon would not have allowed them to make the movie. Andrew Garfield added that he hopes that they will not have the “risk of being taken to court”.Artificial (Image Via Instagram/@neonrated)Artificial is set to speak about the “universal and deeper” anxiety that the world is “feeling about the future” with the exponential progress of this technology. While speaking about not using AI for Artificial, Guadagnino notes that there is significance in bringing life to the “reality,” which is a crucial factor that cannot be done by “sending prompts to a computer”.He also points out the significant harm that AI is causing, especially the mindless destruction of the environment, along with the possibility that “AI can wipe out humanity” within four years.For more such interesting pieces, stay tuned to Soap Central.

scored.body: Sam Altman has warned against turning AI into a god, in an apparent shot at his rivals Anthropic.Mr Altman, chief executive of OpenAI, said that the urge to give “religious force” to artificial intelligence models could be a “real safety issue”.He did not name any particular companies or people in his criticism. But it comes amid increasing concern about the religious and moral questions about AI – and a growing interest in them from some rivals, including Anthropic, maker of Claude."I am very uncomfortable about people trying to ascribe religious force or a surrender of human judgment to AI models, and think it is a real safety issue," Mr Altman said in an X post over the weekend.His comments came shortly after a New York Times article describing the intense lengths that Anthropic has gone to in order to integrate religious thinking into the development of their new models. That included one of the company’s co-founders, Christopher Olah, having reportedly met with a range of religious leaders and discussed ideas including having models undertake a Catholic style confession.Anthropic has suggested that the work with religious leaders is part of a broader effort to ensure that it builds systems that are in line with human views, as well as to consider the wellbeing of any possibly conscious versions of artificial intelligence. But some critics have suggested that it poses a risk of turning the systems into a religious force themselves.“I am disturbed by how some of my fellow AI researchers keep trying to elevate the moral standing of checkpoints and harnesses,” said Jon Barron, principal research scientist at Google Deepmind. “I hope the rest of us on Team Meatbag reject this movement and stay focused on solving real problems and helping actual humans.”The increasing concern over the spiritual nature of AI has also drawn attention from religious thinkers, including the Pope. He has repeatedly warned that artificial intelligence poses a spiritual risk to the people who use it – and repeated similar warnings just days after the New York Times report.“In this era of artificial intelligence, it is becoming urgent to distinguish human art from what machines produce,” Pope Leo said in a tweet. “There is an ontological difference, even before an aesthetic one, between art and what a machine can generate through statistical calculation based on millions of images created by others.“Algorithms lack the spark of humanity. For this reason, the Church wishes to renew an alliance with artists and cultural institutions to safeguard our humanity.”
