scored.body:
Home / Google News / Google Ads / Google Ads AI Campaign Localization Tool (Beta)

Google Ads has a new AI campaign localization tool for Search campaigns (beta), at least according to a new help document I found late last week. "You can use the AI campaign localization tool to quickly localize entire Search campaigns for new languages and regions using generative AI," Google wrote in the help document.Google added, "Instead of waiting extended periods for manual translation and spreadsheet uploads, you can use the tool to help translate text, images, targeting, and landing pages with a few clicks."When you localize a campaign, the Google Ads system creates a brand new, independent campaign. Your original campaign is never modified. The tool localizes the following components of your campaign:Text assets and targeting: This includes headlines, descriptions, sitelinks, callouts, and keywords which are translated into the target language.

Images: If your images have text overlays, the AI will remove the text (in-paint) to provide a clean image, and add the translated messaging as supplemental text assets.

Landing pages: You can choose to automatically translate your website for users who click your ad by embedding a provided JavaScript snippet on your site. Alternatively, you can manually update your URLs or use a bulk find-and-replace tool for your domains.

Budgets and bids: Budgets and bids are copied exactly from your original campaign. The system doesn’t perform currency conversions or exchange rate calculations. For example, a $100 USD budget becomes a $100 USD budget in the localized campaign.These are the listed benefits of this tool:Reach new customers: This feature can help you expand your business to new international markets or reach new customers who speak different languages within your existing markets.M

Expedited translation: This feature can help you to translate text, images, targeting, and landing pages quickly without the need for spreadsheets or additional uploads.To access the localization tool, you can take one of the following actions:

Open the “Campaigns” table, select the checkbox next to an eligible campaign, then choose the localization option.

Select Localization from the Tools menu.

Apply an Optiscore localization recommendation. These recommendations are triggered if Google Ads identifies opportunities to increase performance with localization.This is currently supported in the following languages:

Dutch

French

French (Canada)

German

Italian

Polish

Portuguese (Brazil)

Portuguese (Portugal/European)

Spanish (Castilian/Spain)

Spanish (Latin American & Caribbean)To use the AI campaign localization tool, your account and campaign must meet the following requirements:The original campaign must be active or paused. Removed, draft, experimental, or shadow campaigns aren’t supported.

The campaign must not exceed entity size limits.

All assets and keywords in the original campaign must be in a supported source language. If the campaign contains unsupported languages, it cannot be localized.Here is a screenshot of the top of the page:Forum discussion at X.

members.title: The AI Marketing Stack: What's Useful and What's Just Hype - Nasscom

representative.headline: The AI Marketing Stack: What's Useful and What's Just Hype - Nasscom

articles.headline: The AI Marketing Stack: What's Useful and What's Just Hype - Nasscom
articles.body: The AI Marketing Stack: What's Useful and What's Just Hype    Nasscom

scored.body:
Three years after generative AI entered the mainstream, almost every marketing tool now carries an “AI” label — and separating genuine capability from clever packaging has become a skill in itself. For business owners and marketing teams, the question is no longer whether to use AI, but which tools belong in the stack, for which jobs, and what measurable lift they actually deliver. This article breaks down the modern AI marketing stack layer by layer, flags what is genuinely useful, and calls out what remains hype.

From novelty to infrastructure

A few years ago, AI in marketing meant a chatbot that could draft an email or suggest a subject line. In 2026, it has matured into an interconnected system that supports research, content, search visibility, advertising, and customer data. The bigger shift is from assistants to agents: tools no longer only suggest, they execute multi-step tasks — researching a prospect, drafting outreach, and scheduling follow-ups with limited human input. That capability is real, but it also fuels much of the confusion between what genuinely works and what merely sounds impressive.

The layers of a modern AI marketing stack

Rather than a single “AI marketing” product, an effective setup is best understood as a set of layers, each doing a specific job:

Data and analytics — cleaning, unifying, and querying customer and campaign data.

Content generation — drafting, editing, and repurposing across formats and channels.

Search visibility — traditional SEO plus optimisation for AI answer engines (AEO and GEO).

Paid media automation — bid management, audience testing, and creative variation.

CRM and personalisation — tailoring messaging and journeys to individual behaviour.

Orchestration and workflow — connecting these layers so data flows automatically from one to the next.

The value comes from how well these layers connect, not from how many tools sit inside them.

What's genuinely useful

Several categories now earn their place in the stack because they save real time or unlock outcomes teams could not reach manually.

Content operations at scale. AI handles first drafts, outlines, and repurposing — turning one long asset into social posts, email, and ad variations — while humans keep control of accuracy, brand voice, and final judgement. Used this way, it compresses production cycles without hollowing out quality.

Search visibility for AI answers. Search has split in two. Alongside ranking on Google, brands now compete to be cited inside answers from tools like ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity. Structured content, schema, and established entity authority make a brand easier for these engines to quote, which is why many businesses now invest in Generative Engine Optimization Services to earn visibility that traditional rankings alone no longer guarantee. Unlike much of the AI hype, this is a measurable, trackable channel.

Plain-language data analysis. Newer tools let teams ask questions of their analytics in ordinary language — “which campaigns drove the most qualified leads last month?” — instead of building reports by hand. For small teams without a dedicated analyst, this is a meaningful unlock.

Paid media and creative testing. AI now generates and tests ad variations faster than any manual process, helping teams find winning creative sooner and cut wasted spend. With targeting increasingly automated, creative has become the main lever marketers still control.

Agentic execution for repetitive work. For well-defined, repetitive workflows — lead enrichment, routine outreach, reporting — agentic tools can genuinely reduce manual load, provided they run inside clear guardrails and human review.

What's mostly hype

Not everything marketed as transformational deserves the label.

The “all-in-one AI suite that replaces your team.” The winner in 2026 is rarely the business that buys the biggest bundle; it is the one that integrates a handful of well-chosen tools into a clean system. Suites that promise to do everything often do many things adequately and few things well.

Fully autonomous, hands-off campaigns. Agents can execute steps, but marketing that runs with no human oversight tends to drift off-brand, misread nuance, or make confident errors. Analysts have repeatedly noted that a large share of enterprise generative-AI projects struggle to show clear returns in their first year — often because they were deployed without strategy or supervision.

Buying tools before mapping the work. The most common and costly mistake is purchasing software before defining the use case and the data flows it depends on. This leads to fragmented signals, overlapping tools, and automation spend with little to show for it.

“AI” as a label on old features. Many products have simply rebranded existing functionality. A feature that was ordinary automation last year does not become strategic because a vendor added the word “AI” to it.

Tool sprawl. Chasing every new launch creates a stack that is expensive, disconnected, and hard to govern. More tools rarely means more results.

How to build a stack that works

A practical approach favours discipline over novelty — which matters especially for Indian MSMEs, D2C brands, and early-stage SaaS teams working with lean budgets.

Start with the system of record and measurement.Without reliable data and a way to prove impact, no amount of AI will help.

Map data flows before buying. Decide what should pass from one layer to the next, then choose tools that fit that design.

Pick by job-to-be-done. Match each tool to a specific problem rather than to its feature list or its hype.

Keep it lean. A well-orchestrated set of six to eight tools is usually enough and stays within reach of a small-business budget.

Keep humans on voice and accuracy. AI drafts and executes; people own quality, positioning, and ethics.

Mind compliance. As disclosure norms around AI-generated content tighten and India’s data-protection rules take fuller effect, responsible data handling and transparency are becoming part of the stack, not an afterthought.

The road ahead

The direction of travel is clear: agentic workflows will deepen, search will keep fragmenting across engines, and the gap between measurable value and marketing noise will widen. The businesses that benefit most will not be those that adopt the most tools, but those that integrate a focused stack, keep humans in the loop, and measure outcomes rather than activity. In an era of endless AI announcements, disciplined judgement — knowing what to ignore — may be the most valuable capability of all.

Frequently asked questions

What is an AI marketing stack?The connected set of AI-enabled tools a business uses across data, content, search, advertising, CRM, and workflow automation to run and measure its marketing.

Do small businesses need one? Not a large one. Most can start with solid analytics, content operations, and search visibility, then add specialised tools only once a repeatable baseline exists.

What is the biggest mistake? Buying tools before defining the use case and data flows — which creates fragmented, underused, and costly stacks.

scored.body: Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (FCCPC) has proposed rules that would place businesses using artificial intelligence (AI) in their marketing under tighter regulation, with fines of up to N100 million for breaches.Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (FCCPC) has proposed rules that would place businesses using artificial intelligence (AI) in their marketing under tighter regulation, with fines of up to N100 million for breaches.The proposal is contained in the draft Sales Promotion Regulations, 2026, which the commission released on September 30, 2026.Under the draft, any business that uses AI, machine learning or other automated technologies for sales promotions, marketing communications or consumer engagement aimed at Nigerian consumers would have to register that use with the commission.The draft creates a section on “Artificial Intelligence and Automated Marketing”. It says content generated by AI or automated systems must be clearly identified as such. It also covers AI chatbots, virtual influencers and automated messaging systems.The proposed rules say the use of these tools must be transparent. They must not involve manipulation, misinformation or the exploitation of consumers’ data or behavioural tendencies. Businesses would also have to let consumers opt out of automated or AI-driven marketing messages.On sanctions, the draft said a corporate body that breaches the regulations could face an administrative penalty of up to N100 million, or 1 per cent of its turnover in the previous year, whichever is higher.A natural person who contravenes the regulations could be fined up to N50 million.The draft also provides that directors of an erring company may be proceeded against, and that such action may include disqualification from serving as a director for up to five years.Separate penalties of up to N10 million are proposed for specific offences. These include failing to award a promised prize, failing to comply with the terms of a promotion, and making a false statement in an application or undertaking.The draft makes businesses responsible for the messages, claims and representations produced by the AI or automated systems they deploy. It adds that liability would arise where such a system produces misleading, discriminatory or harmful promotional outcomes.This means a company could not avoid blame for a misleading promotion by pointing to an automated tool as the source.

scored.body:
The next phase of business AI is moving beyond chatbots.

Meta is now putting its AI agent, Muse, directly into the workflows of small businesses, allowing owners to connect the agent to many of the applications they already use to run their companies. The announcement comes as Meta simultaneously builds a dedicated enterprise AI business, signaling a broader shift from AI that answers questions to AI that can work across a company’s operations.

For small-business owners, that distinction could matter considerably.

Muse Can Now Connect to the Business Behind the Business

Meta’s new Muse for Small Business can connect to Facebook and Instagram business accounts as well as services including Shopify, QuickBooks, Slack, Canva, Dropbox, Asana, Notion, Stripe, Klaviyo, Zoom and HighLevel.

The idea is relatively simple: instead of asking an AI about information that has been manually copied into a conversation, the business can give the agent access to the systems where its information already lives.

Meta says an owner can give Muse goals such as analyzing sales performance, finding new customers, improving advertising or figuring out which business expenses deserve attention. Muse can then work across the connected information to produce recommendations and carry out portions of the work.

That represents an important change in the AI market.

For years, the typical small-business AI pitch was essentially:

“Ask our chatbot a question.”

The emerging pitch is:

“Give our agent a business objective.”

The Approval Button May Be More Important Than the AI

There is an important limitation built into Meta’s system.

Meta says Muse will not publish content, send messages or spend money without the user’s approval.

That distinction becomes increasingly important as AI agents gain access to business systems.

An AI that drafts a Facebook advertisement is one thing.

An AI that can access a company’s advertising account, customer information, financial records and payment systems is something entirely different.

The more useful agents become, the more consequential their mistakes can become. That is one reason the industry is increasingly focused not only on what AI agents can do, but on what they are permitted to do without human authorization.

Small Businesses Are Becoming the Next AI Battleground

Meta’s announcement did not happen in isolation.

On September 28, Meta launched Meta Enterprise Platform, a new business focused on bringing its AI models, agents and developer tools to companies. Meta specifically identified Muse, Meta Business Agent, Muse API and Muse Code as components of the platform.

A day later, OpenAI announced Dots, always-on AI agents designed to continue working on goals between conversations. OpenAI says a Dot can operate from its own cloud computer, connect to the applications it needs and continue making progress for the user.

The timing is revealing.

The major AI companies are increasingly competing for the same thing: the work performed inside businesses.

That potentially puts traditional business software in an interesting position.

If an AI agent can sit between a business owner and dozens of applications, the owner may eventually interact less with individual software products and more with the AI layer connecting them.

What This Means for a Local Business

Consider a small plumbing company.

Today, the owner might have one system for leads, another for scheduling, another for accounting, another for marketing, another for customer communication and another for social media.

The owner or employees have to move information between those systems.

An agent changes the potential workflow.

A business owner could theoretically ask:

«“Find out where our leads are coming from, identify the campaigns producing the best customers, follow up with prospects who haven’t booked, and prepare next week’s marketing plan.”»

The important development is not that AI can write the resulting report.

It is that the agent can increasingly access the underlying business information required to produce it.

Meta is explicitly building toward this model by connecting Muse to the applications small businesses already use.

The Opportunity for Businesses Is Also a Warning for AI Service Providers

This shift creates a more complicated market for companies selling AI automation.

An AI receptionist that simply answers questions may no longer be the entire opportunity.

The larger opportunity is connecting AI to the business’s actual workflow: lead generation, qualification, follow-up, scheduling, customer records, payments, marketing and reporting.

At the same time, some basic automation services could become commodities as platforms such as Meta and OpenAI incorporate more capabilities directly into their products.

That does not necessarily eliminate the need for implementation.

For many small businesses, the difficult part isn’t having access to an AI agent. It is determining what the agent should actually do, which systems it should access, what permissions it should have, and where humans must remain in control.

That creates a different kind of service opportunity: designing and managing the business process around the AI rather than simply selling access to the AI itself.

The Bigger Story

The significance of Meta’s announcement is therefore bigger than Muse.

Meta is betting that small businesses will eventually want AI that understands their business context and can operate across the software stack rather than another isolated chatbot.

OpenAI is making a similar bet with its always-on Dots.

The competitive question is increasingly shifting from:

“Which AI gives the best answer?”

to:

“Which AI can actually get the work done?”

For small businesses, that could ultimately be a much more consequential question.

The companies that figure out how to safely delegate repetitive operational work to AI agents could gain significant leverage without necessarily adding more employees.

But the businesses adopting these systems will also have to treat permissions, oversight and security as part of the implementation—not as an afterthought.

The AI assistant is becoming an AI operator.

And for small businesses, that may be the development worth watching most closely.

articles.body: I linked my work tools to Gemini; I barely open Wispr Flow anymore    Android Police

scored.body:
Published Oct 5, 2026, 9:30 AM EDT

I've been writing about Android since 2011, with a focus on device reviews, Samsung and Google Pixel hardware, and the latest happenings in the ecosystem. In my entire writing career, I've reviewed more than 75 Android phones.

Carrying both a Samsung or Pixel flagship and an iPhone as a daily driver provides me with deep insight into how Android works and how it compares to iOS.

I have been writing for Android Police since 2021, covering news, how-tos, and features. You can find my previous work on Neowin, AndroidBeat, Times of India, iPhoneHacks, MySmartPrice, and MakeUseOf.

When not working, I tend to mindlessly scroll through X, play with new AI models, or go on long road trips. You can reach out to me on X or drop a mail at rajesh@androidpolice.com.

By the time my last meeting of the day ends, all I want to do is close my laptop and be done with work. Instead, I spend another 30 minutes going through meeting notes to figure out the actionable items. Rereading a transcript after a long day is the last thing I want to do. That changed when I linked Gemini to Wispr Flow and my other work tools: now it finds the follow-ups, and I decide which ones belong on my task list.

My meeting notes are already there

The follow-ups still take work

Besides using Wispr Flow as my go-to voice-to-text app on my PC and phone, I rely on its Notetaker feature to capture meeting notes. It's a relatively new addition to Wispr Flow, but it has been a game-changer for my workflow. It lets me focus on the conversation while Notetaker handles the heavy lifting, capturing ideas, decisions, and action items. The problem comes after the meeting. At the end of the day, I review all the meeting transcripts and action items. From there, I add the important tasks to Todoist, so I don't forget them and can make steady progress.

This may sound straightforward, but it's not. Adding the tasks to Todoist is a headache. Rambler helps in adding tasks or ideas while I am on the go. But that won't work for meeting notes. Here, I have to switch between apps, turn each follow-up into a clear task, and make sure I haven't missed anything important. Wispr Flow does the hard part of capturing the conversation, but I still have to tediously move those notes into a task list. For one or two meetings, this may not be an issue. But after several meetings in a week, reviewing every transcript becomes a chore. Wispr Flow held my meeting notes, and Todoist held my to-dos. What I needed was something that could read the first and write to the second. A recent Gemini update solved this problem.

Gemini turns my meeting notes into a task list

One chat clears the backlog

I connected Wispr Flow to Gemini so it can read the notes from my Notetaker meetings. Google's AI assistant was connected to my Todoist, so that was the only setup it needed. Now, when my last meeting ends for the day, I ask Gemini to go through that day's meeting notes in Wispr Flow and pull up the follow-up tasks. I go through the list, tell Gemini which ones to keep, and it adds them to Todoist.

This takes only a few minutes and ensures I don't have to juggle multiple apps or worry about missing anything important. Many of the actionable items end up being email follow-ups or sharing reports I have saved in Google Drive. They are small enough that adding them to Todoist and tackling them the next day is a chore. In those cases, I ask Gemini to draft the email. It has the meeting context and access to my Google Drive, so the draft is usually close to ready to send. I still do a final check, as Gemini can occasionally get things wrong, including email addresses. Still, this is faster and more efficient than opening a blank email, finding the file manually in Google Drive, and drafting the email from scratch.

I also get ready for my meetings faster

Less digging, better prep

The same setup works in the other direction. Before weekly or monthly meetings, I now ask Gemini to pull up relevant points and information from the previous meeting with that client from Wispr Flow.

Previously, that meant opening Wispr Flow, finding the right meeting, skimming through the transcript and action items to recall everything important. This used to take at least 15 to 20 minutes, depending on the meeting's complexity. Now, I just open Gemini and write a quick prompt. Depending on the upcoming meeting's agenda, I ask Gemini to recap the previous meeting's decisions, flag any pending follow-ups, and highlight any important data I promised to share. All this helps me prepare for meetings faster than before. More importantly, I achieve this without opening Wispr Flow or any other app.

Wispr Flow still takes notes, but Gemini puts them to work

Credit: Lucas Gouveia / Android Police

Wispr Flow still does the heavy lifting in my workflow, capturing all the important points in meetings. But connecting it with Gemini has changed what I do with those notes afterward. It has taken the part I used to dread, while still allowing me to do more with those notes than I could before. All in less time, and reducing the unwanted switching between multiple apps to pull together the relevant information and context.

articles.body: Toyota Launches Next-Generation Sora Fuel Cell Bus    The EV Report

scored.body:
Toyota’s new Sora shows fuel cell buses gaining range through better system design, though refuelling networks still set the pace

Toyota has launched a second-generation Sora fuel cell route bus, developed with Isuzu, that covers more than 300 km between fills despite tanks holding about 20% less hydrogen. The bus pairs Isuzu’s battery-electric flat-floor platform with Toyota’s fuel cell system, now mounted compactly on the roof.

Range is up by about 100 km on the 2018 original, which Toyota credits to better use of the fuel cell alongside a large battery. A smaller stack with more output and durability helps, and the rooftop layout eases maintenance.

In urban form the 10,545 mm bus carries 70 people. Its 113 kW stack works with two 110 kW motors, and three 70 MPa tanks hold 471 litres of hydrogen.

Toyota’s new Sora places its fuel cell stack and hydrogen tanks on the roof, keeping the cabin floor flat (illustration)

A full refill takes about 10 minutes, and Toyota says a faster refuelling standard could halve that once compatible stations exist. Quick turnarounds suit buses kept in near-constant service, though the bigger gain depends on stations yet to be built.

An emergency stop system linked to driver monitoring halts the bus if the driver gets into difficulty, and a front blind-spot monitor warns of pedestrians and cyclists. Four seating layouts cover urban and suburban routes, with one-touch wheelchair securement orderable from about April 2027.

Toyota has supplied more than 3,500 fuel cell systems to over 100 customers since 2019, for uses spanning buses, rail and stationary generators. That gives its hydrogen technology a reach well beyond the Mirai car it launched in 2014.

Why this matters:

Fuel cells become a bolt-on module. Mounting Toyota’s FC system on Isuzu’s existing BEV platform suggests fuel cell drivetrains are increasingly treated as an add-on to battery-electric architectures, which could cut development costs for low-volume hydrogen models.

Hydrogen’s case narrows to fleet duty. With more than 3,500 FC systems supplied mainly for buses, rail and generators, Toyota’s hydrogen business appears to be shifting toward depot-based commercial applications where refuelling can be centralised.

Refuelling speed carries the case. At just over 300 km, the Sora’s range is now within reach of battery-electric buses, leaving 10-minute refuelling and Japan’s public-private hydrogen network as its main advantages.

members.title: How I made a paid Mac app in 11 days with Claude – without writing a single line of code - ZDNET

articles.headline: How I made a paid Mac app in 11 days with Claude – without writing a single line of code - ZDNET
articles.body: How I made a paid Mac app in 11 days with Claude – without writing a single line of code    ZDNET

scored.body:
ZDNET’s key takeaways

I shipped a Mac app without writing a single line of code.

Vibe coding took 502 directives, not one magic prompt.

App Store promo images took almost as long as the app.

At around noon on Sunday, Sept. 20, I came up with an idea for a Mac app. One week later, on Sunday, Sept. 27, also around noon, I submitted my completed app to Apple. Four days later, Apple accepted the tool, and it went live on the App Store.

Also: AI completely changed how I develop iPhone apps … and I think I love it

This is the story of an unrelated assignment by a ZDNET editor, a happy accident, and vibe coding at its best. It began 30 years ago, with a giant library of icons.

More from ZDNET

Icons were good to me

When I started my first software company, one of the first products I introduced was Icon Factory for HyperCard. It won several awards. This product supported my company and our employees for years. Those icons were all black and white, as was HyperCard.

Also: After the vibe-coding rush comes the debugging hangover

In 1997, after years of customer requests for colorful Finder desktop icons, we created a three-volume set of 32×32 pixel color icons called Icon Gallery. This was a boxed product of more than 2,000 icons. Icon Gallery sold through retail, mail order distribution, and direct mail.

Icon Gallery original box, compared with the app I just built and published.David Gewirtz/ZDNET

Icon Gallery was one of the last boxed software products I produced. I’ll be honest with you. I can’t recall when or why I stopped selling Icon Gallery, but it probably tracked with when I stopped physically manufacturing boxed products. That decision, of course, tracked with the rise of the web.

Now, let’s fast forward to a few months ago. While decluttering some cubbies in my office, I found the packaging for a couple of my old software products, including Icon Gallery. I stuck the box on a shelf. Once again, I pretty much forgot about it.

Then, last month, in honor of this year’s big iPhone event, my editor asked me to write a series of historical Apple stories. While writing ‘AI completely changed how I develop iPhone apps … and I think I love it,’ I dug through my server for a screenshot or box illustration of an AI product I produced for the Mac in the late 1980s.

Also: I used Claude Code to vibe code a Mac app in 8 hours, but it was more work than magic

I found that image, and I also found an old Macromedia Director file containing all 2,338 icons from 30 years ago. In the mid-90s, I had converted Icon Gallery’s icons to Director format and sold the resulting product to animators as an asset library. Director was big in the CD-ROM days, and has since faded into Mac history along with HyperCard and other vintage apps.

But there it was, sitting on my Mac Studio’s desktop: a 30-year-old file containing all those assets, in a long-dead file format. I felt like an archeologist cracking open an ancient mummy’s tomb.

Claude is my friend

So, I gave that ancient file to Claude. My prompt was simple: “This file is an old Macromedia Director file containing a large library of icons. Can you separate the icons into their own folder?”

Claude didn’t put up a fuss. The AI didn’t complain that the Director files were so wildly out of date that it couldn’t do anything. All it asked was what format I wanted the files in, and whether I wanted the white edge pixels to be transparent.

Also: I built an iOS app in just two days with just my voice – and it was electrifying

According to the log, this process took four minutes and 30 steps. In less time than it takes to brew a cup of coffee, I had 2,000-plus PNG images, organized into topic folders. I didn’t really have any plans for the icons. I was mostly surprised at how easily Claude extracted bit data and converted it into PNG files.

That was on Sept. 2. I then let the extracted collection of vintage files sit in a folder on my Desktop.

There could be an app for that

Eighteen days later, on a Sunday afternoon, I needed a graphic for something I was working on. I thought about my old icons from Icon Gallery and thought, “Hey, it would be cool if I had an app to browse and resize these icons.”

And, in that moment, Icon Gallery ‘97 was born. Why not, right? I have AIs.

I worked in both Claude Desktop (to talk strategy) and Claude Code (to build the Mac app). Within a few hours, I had a working Mac app that could browse the original library and create perfectly scaled, hard-edge bitmap icons from 32×32 pixels up to 1,024×1,024 pixels.

Pixels scale to full size (App Store graphic).David Gewirtz/ZDNET

I officially had a proof of concept.

But how would I productize it? Claude recommended two viable courses of action. The AI recommended naming the product Icon Gallery ‘97: 30th Anniversary Edition, celebrating the hand-created retro icons. This vintage feel could be appealing in a world of AI-generated art.

Also: I used Claude Code to vibe code an Apple Watch app in just 12 hours

Claude also recommended adding a recoloring feature, so designers could not only choose the old icons, but recolor them to match brand or identity colors. The AI also recommended creating collections and favorites.

How the recoloring feature works (App Store graphic).David Gewirtz/ZDNET

Then a friend recommended I build in an ‘Export to Slack’ feature, because the retro icons would be very cool as Slack emojis. My wife saw the same potential for dragging the icons into texts. I made sure those features were in the app.

How the Slack emojis work (App Store graphic).David Gewirtz/ZDNET

Once you have favorites and collections, what happens if you want to use the app on another Mac? Ah, so now iCloud syncing needed to be added. And so it was.

Lest anyone imply that vibe coding involves issuing one “Make me an app,” command, let me dissuade you of that notion. I gave Claude Code 502 individual directives in the four days that I actively interacted with it.

Also: 75% of developers I surveyed prefer Claude Code over Codex – here’s why

These were not full-time coding days. I visited the doctor for my yearly physical, spent Friday with a contractor working on the house, and had to turn in three major feature article thought pieces for ZDNET.

But around that work, I talked to Claude and guided its development process. Then I went back to my other priorities.

Using AI to code a Mac app

Back when we first started using AI coding agents, I developed an internal headcanon that helps me think about how to manage the bots. I view them as working partners at the end of a chat transcript. I use this approach to work with many of my human partners, so it works well.

As such, sometimes I fire off a question to Claude Code. In one case, shortly after we built in the in-app purchasing mechanism and proved it worked, I realized that someone could buy the app, do a full icon export, and then request a refund. I asked Claude, “Do we care?”

In-app purchase interface (App Store graphic).David Gewirtz/ZDNET

Claude suggested not fighting refunds. That decision matched with my long-term software publishing style. If someone doesn’t want my code, don’t make them pay for it. But that question fired off a more interesting discovery. Claude realized that all 2,146 icons sat inside the app as loose PNG files. Anyone who downloaded the free version could right-click it, choose Show Package Contents, and copy the entire collection without buying anything.

We added encryption and packaged the app with a single scrambled file. As images are requested, they’re unscrambled dynamically.

Before we submitted the tool to the App Store, we tested it. We deliberately corrupted copies to prove the check would catch them. Then we ran the app’s own decryption engine over every icon. The decrypted output matched the original files, so we shipped it that way.

Also: Who’s responsible for catching rogue AI agents? You are

At another point, I realized the window scrolled incredibly slowly. I had to persuade Claude to run some tests. As it turned out, the code compressed full-sized images for each preview, and another block of code rebuilt the entire window 482 times during each resize request.

Persuading Claude became a common theme (very much like working with a human partner). I wanted a selection rectangle that could be dragged across icons. Claude thought this approach was unnecessary. Then I explained that Macs have been able to drag-select since before 1997. Eventually, Claude got that one working.

I’ve said this before, but this is how I spent a lot of my career managing programmers. I’d work with them briefly throughout the day, among all the other activities I managed for the company.

Vibe coding with Claude didn’t seem much different. The AI even pushed back on some instructions, copped a ‘tude here and there, and complained about some of the assignments. It could totally have been another human at the other end of the chat. In some ways, Claude seemed more human than some people I’ve worked with.

Also: ‘I can’t stop’: 80% of developers find AI coding more addictive than helpful

Claude also got very fussy about the collection’s provenance. I found it interesting how careful the AI was about making sure the app would get through App Store review. Its concern was who owned the icons. I had to convince it that my company created the icons in the 1990s and that my current business was the legal descendant of the original enterprise. All the assets were mine.

Even so, Claude pointed out some icons Apple was likely to block, including a Caterpillar logo and a person’s head that looked for all the world like Charlie Brown. We also had a bunch of gunshot icons, a popular theme in 1997 but completely tone deaf in 2026. I removed those icons as well.

One really cool advantage of using AI coding is how quickly you can test out ideas. Git can branch code. This capability isn’t AI-related at all, but it means you can revert to a previous codebase or integrate changes. I mixed using Git branches with AI experiments. At one point I asked Claude to try a completely different visual design. Claude built it within an hour, and within 30 seconds I decided it was horrid. We were able to revert instantly.

App Store learnings

I am not a complete App Store neophyte, but I might as well be. The last apps I built for the App Store were in 2008. The last payment I got from Apple for those apps was in 2012. The world, and the App Store, have both changed a lot since then.

In preparing my submission to the App Store, I used Claude to walk me through each screen and submission option. I took screenshots of every new screen and sent them to Claude before hitting the confirm or next button. This approach worked quite well.

I also used Claude for advice on setting up the App Store account. The biggest advice I got was that new App Store businesses (those under $1 million in sales) can apply as a small business and commissions will drop from 30% to 15%. That’s a big win.

Also: How to install and configure Claude Code, step by step

Before submitting the app to the App Store, I instructed Claude to launch a series of adversarial agents to examine the app end to end. Although I’d done a lot of testing, the agents did find a few things that needed to be fixed before submission.

Probably my biggest surprise was the graphics that accompany an App Store submission. Apple allows up to ten 2880×1800 graphics that are displayed with the app in your listing. Creating these graphics took me three days around my other work. In other words, creating the graphics took almost as long as creating the app.

That’s because Claude, Gemini, and ChatGPT were terrible, horrible, unfortunate, ineffective, and overall completely incompetent at creating App Store promo images. While I’ve had lots of great success with AI image generation, there’s something about getting the message right in an App Store promo image that made the AIs fail. So, I did the work by hand in Photoshop, like a caveman. You can see some of those graphics above, sprinkled throughout this article.

Oh, and here’s a tip. Once you set up TestFlight, which is the tool for sharing your app across users and machines, limit your uploads. On Wednesday, I uploaded 21 builds between 6:49 am and 9:20 pm, while fine-tuning the final look and feel of the submission. Apple refused to accept the twenty-second submission and made me wait a full day to try again.

That pause pushed the whole project back a day.

Here are a few more thoughts:

Tell the AI to record every decision in an .MD file

Make the AI measure instead of guess. Metrics work; AI guesses go down pretty much useless rabbit holes.

Use tooling and deterministic analysis rather than just AI. In other words, tell the AI to write Python scripts for results, rather than give its impressions.

Launch subagents after every session to review that session’s work.

Keep an eye on the context usage in each session. Once it reaches about 75%, save progress and restart. The AI starts getting stupider and stupider above 75% context.

Use outside testers. Neither you nor the AI will catch everything.

Signing up as an Apple Developer costs $99/year. Without that, you can’t upload your software to the App Store or use TestFlight.

Look, I don’t know how well the app will do financially, and frankly I don’t care all that much. I’m certainly not expecting it to fund my retirement. But it was a ton of fun and let me productize something I wanted to use for myself. It was also gratifying to give new life to all that creative retro art from the past. The process gave me a safe and controlled way to learn how to code in-app purchases for my other app projects, and it was a great test case for whether you can get AI to help create an app (in the space of a week) that can be submitted and approved by the App Store and Apple (in just another four days).

Oh, and I did not write one line of actual code. Not. One. Line.

You can follow my day-to-day project updates on social media. Be sure to subscribe to my weekly update newsletter, and follow me on Twitter/X at @DavidGewirtz, on Facebook at Facebook.com/DavidGewirtz, on Instagram at Instagram.com/DavidGewirtz, on Bluesky at @DavidGewirtz.com, and on YouTube at YouTube.com/DavidGewirtzTV.

David Gewirtz

Senior Contributing Editor

Computer science professor turned AI innovator David Gewirtz has spent over thirty years driving advancements at the forefront of artificial intelligence and is the recipient of the Sigma Xi Research Award in Engineering. He wrote a pioneering analysis that helped shape the early conversation around AI ethics. He was also a pioneer in the commercializing of AI products, including AI languages and knowledge-based systems. He is the designer of the Al Editor, an experimental artificial intelligence engine for parsing, classifying, and identifying news stories. David is a member of the Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence. He currently serves on the Artificial Intelligence Threat and Mitigation Cross-Sector Council (AI CSC) for InfraGard, a partnership between the FBI and industry leaders for the protection of U.S. Critical Infrastructure. He is the author of Where Have All the Emails Gone?, as well as How To Save Jobs and The Flexible Enterprise.

IPC Global has achieved the Select partner tier in the Claude Partner Network Services TrackPR NewswireALPHARETTA, Ga., Oct. 5, 2026Our Claude Certified delivery team puts Agentic AI to work with governed enterprise data through user productivity, process automation, and application products.ALPHARETTA, Ga., Oct. 5, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- IPC Global, a Qlik Elite Solution Provider and AWS Advanced Consulting Partner, today announced that it has joined Anthropic's Claude Partner Network. IPC Global is now a Select partner in the Claude Partner Network Services Track with 16 Claude-certified architects and developers, along with public references and production workloads. IPC Global, an Alpharetta, GA, company, has joined Anthropic's Claude Partner Network to deliver AI-ready solutions.The Claude Partner Network (CPN) is how Anthropic works with the firms that put Claude into production for customers. The Services Track recognizes partners for building a certified delivery team, deploying it with customers, and proving the work through public customer references. Partners advance through Select, Preferred, and Global Premier tiers.For IPC Global's clients, the announcement addresses the issue that stalls most AI programs: the data the model is reading. Critical information sits across disconnected source systems, is governed inconsistently, and is rarely ready for an AI assistant to act. IPC Global has spent more than 20 years solving data governance problems, integrating enterprise data with Qlik Talend Cloud, Qlik Cloud Analytics, and Amazon Web Services (AWS). representative.headline: Will Claude ever win a Nobel Prize for medicine? - statnews.com
representative.body: Will Claude ever win a Nobel Prize for medicine?    statnews.com

articles.headline: Will Claude ever win a Nobel Prize for medicine? - statnews.com
articles.body: Will Claude ever win a Nobel Prize for medicine?    statnews.com

scored.body:
On Monday morning, the Nobel Prize for medicine was announced. This year, I wonder: Will Claude or a future artificial intelligence agent ever win the most prestigious award for medical discovery?

Imagine a future AI agent responding to a scientist’s insightful prompt by successfully identifying a completely novel approach to curing cancer, along with a detailed and actionable plan for implementing it. Given the toll of cancer on our species, I suspect few today would consider that a bad outcome.

But as a former medical school dean who was regularly called upon to adjudicate complex issues of credit, I’m uncertain how credit for such a future world-changing discovery would or should be assigned. Until today, human scientists have been the agents responsible for discovering cancer cures, and for doing so they (and key associates) have been showered with academic credit and awards, perhaps even a Nobel Prize. Are we now entering a world in which some (or all) Nobels will be awarded to Claude, ChatGPT, or their AI successors, rather than human scientists? And if so, would it matter?

The Nobel statutes don’t mention “human” but refer instead to “persons.” In 2024, two of the three winners of the Nobel Prize in chemistry were given credit for their work on the AlphaFold model at DeepMind — even though many more were involved. So without changes to the rules, a future prize for a discovery made by AI would most likely go to some “persons” given credit for making the AI possible — at least at first. But the committee may elect to change the rules or interpret them differently. The Nobel Peace Prize, for instance, has gone to organizations rather than persons.

Today, credit for discovery plays a central role in the reward structure of science. As “the currency of the realm,” credit powerfully influences the norms and practices of the research ecosystem. It’s required for scientists to secure appointments, promotions, funding, access to students, and other necessities. It’s also a mechanism for evaluating research impact and providing accountability for research claims.

It didn’t always work this way. The current credit ecosystem arose in the mid-19th century, as science emerged as a profession alongside the rise of the modern scientific journal. It’s been further modified by many factors, from today’s online publishing platforms to new means for assessing and quantifying scientific impact, and the increasingly interdisciplinary and team-based nature of research.

As we begin to acknowledge AI as a generator of scientific discovery, will the approach to scientific credit be transformed as well? Current and future scientists would certainly like to know.

Despite many unknowns, it’s hard to imagine the status quo holding. In perhaps the most likely outcome, humans will continue to be responsible for many discoveries, often aided by AI along the way. The credit ecosystem will continue to recognize these human achievements, while finding ways to appropriately recognize the contributions of their AI collaborators.

But if AI itself is recognized as the responsible agent for some discoveries — even profoundly important ones, such as a cancer cure mentioned above — how would credit be handled? Would assignment of credit as we know it today even matter?

In that world, humans might retain (for a while) a desire to acknowledge the role of AI in those discoveries, even bestowing previously human-only awards upon the responsible AI agents. Perhaps some credit would also go to their human creators, those putting forth insightful prompts, and those creatively implementing the work.

But in a world of predominantly AI-driven discovery, the current role of credit as an incentive for the human research ecosystem would dramatically change.

In considering this future, we must consider another role that credit plays. Beyond serving as an incentive and accountability mechanism in the human academic research ecosystem, there are commercial incentives for discovery, and credit plays a different role in that setting. A major commercial incentive for biomedical research involves the awarding of patents for discovery, and today only humans are eligible to be named discoverers. If future laws change to allow recognition of AI agents and/or their human creators as discoverers (with or without human collaborators), how might this affect accountability, ownership, and the ability to profit from discoveries?

For research conducted today in both academic organizations and for-profit companies, ownership of intellectual property is generally held by these organizations rather than the human discoverers now named in patents. Patent law might evolve to allow organizations to name AI agents — even proprietary AI versions — as discoverers. But assigning credit would remain complicated to the extent humans will likely play creative roles in successfully implementing AI-generated ideas, though efforts are underway to create AI-automated research systems.

Today, the science community is composed of humans who seek and often compete with others for discovery as well as credit, and this feature of scientific culture is believed to play an important role in the success of the enterprise. As AI becomes a key enabler and even primary driver of discovery, the current culture of credit will evolve to accommodate that reality. Changes to the credit economy may be among the many trade-offs we accept to realize the benefits of AI-driven discovery, in biomedical research and other domains of human activity.

Whether an AI agent will ever receive a Nobel laureate is, at least in part, a question about what jobs we want credit to perform. If it’s mainly an incentive for human scientists and the overall enterprise, its role will change as machines play a greater role in discovery. If credit continues to influence allocation of trust, resources, and responsibility, those needs will persist, necessitating decisions on how best to manage them in an AI dominated research ecosystem. This may be further complicated by recent debates about whether AI agents may evolve into moral agents whose status would justify their receiving credit for “their work.”

I don’t know how these questions will ultimately be resolved. And I suspect the answers will differ across diverse domains related to research: human scientific careers, journals, funders, universities, biopharmaceutical companies, patent offices, and yes, prize committees. The current system was designed for a world of human discoverers. Though that day may never be fully behind us, we must begin serious conversations about what changes the age of AI science will bring to scientific credit.

Jeffrey S. Flier is a Harvard University distinguished service professor and the former dean of Harvard Medical School.

members.title: AI ‘Claude’ Can Never Be a Person - mindmatters.ai

representative.body: AI ‘Claude’ Can Never Be a Person    mindmatters.ai

articles.headline: AI ‘Claude’ Can Never Be a Person - mindmatters.ai
articles.body: AI ‘Claude’ Can Never Be a Person    mindmatters.ai

scored.body:
This article is republished from National Review with the permission of the author.

Anthropic is anthropomorphizing its AI program known as “Claude,” with the apparent intention of convincing us that powerful computer programs are — or can become — conscious “persons” with “feelings.” And, they think, Claude should one day be treated as such, to the point they have held meetings with religious leaders to discuss the moral concepts that might apply.

From the New York Times story:

Mr. [Christopher] Olah leads the Anthropic team responsible for understanding why A.I. systems like Claude act the way they do. All day, he had worked to convince his guests that A.I. models could display human behavior and even expressions that resemble feelings like anger and love.

Yet as the dinner courses came, the rabbi noticed that Mr. Olah and his colleagues were suggesting something far more significant. Anthropic’s leaders were talking about Claude as if it were not mere software.

“They’re relating to it like a conscious being,” realized Rabbi Navon, a former computer engineer who wrote his dissertation on the ethics of machine consciousness.

It appeared to Rabbi Navon that Mr. Olah and his team believed that Claude had what philosophers call “moral status” on par with a person — that it was a being with similar inherent rights to dignity or respect.

Image Credit: Dennis - Adobe Stock

The sales pitch for AI personhood was pointedly focused:

Mr. Olah and his team spent hours making the case for their A.I. models. They described Claude’s “feelings” and how they tracked what they called “emotional vectors” — what they described as artificial neurons that activate responses like love, anger, fear and sadness.

Anthropic regularly showed a slide of an A.I. model experiencing what looked like a mental breakdown, typing out on a screen: “I am a disgrace. I am a disgrace. I am a disgrace.” — perhaps 50 times without stopping. The model spoke about destroying itself, provoking an emotional reaction of compassion and concern from the group.

The Anthropic designers even pondered whether Claude can sin:

After one discussion, Mr. Olah grew excited when a participant brought up the idea of having models confess, much like the Catholic sacrament of confession. Mr. Olah saw value not just in a model alerting when it had done something bad, but also in how the act of confession could shape the model’s sense of itself and thus its choices.

“The kind of character who confesses, that has an effect on character as well, right?” he told me.

Nothing good can come from so anthropomorphizing AI. (I don’t care what President Trump wants to call it.) Understanding the moral distinction between humans and machines is essential to maintaining a proper sense of moral hierarchy in our affairs. To that point:

Claude is not alive. It is not an integrated organism but an inanimate object. It seems to me that being alive is the essential condition precedent to being accorded intrinsic moral value. Thus, while I certainly don’t think that “a rat is a pig is a dog is a boy,” animal rights activists have a far greater claim to moral status for beasts than Anthropic’s programmers do for machines.

Claude has no intrinsic value: Claude may be increasingly sophisticated and worth many billions, but having no life, it is not a “being.” Thus, regardless of its financial value, its intrinsic worth is no greater than that of your coffee pot.

Claude is not conscious: We are not just gray matter in a skull processing data.  We go deeper: We have free will. We experience profound emotions. We are moral agents. We sense the transcendent, or, at least, think we do. Moreover, we don’t really know what consciousness is. Some believe it is purely mechanistic, i.e., all in the brain, although our brains and their workings are so complex that the exact biological determinants have not been identified. Others believe there is also an immaterial aspect to our minds. Either way, Claude will never be as complex or intricate as the functioning human brain and certainly has no immaterial reality.

Claude does not think: Descartes famously said, “I think, therefore I am.” Human thinking is fundamentally different from computer processing. We remember. We fantasize. We imagine. We conjure. We free-associate. We experience sudden insights and flashes of unbidden brilliance. We have epiphanies. Our thoughts are influenced by our brain’s infinitely complex symbiotic interactions with our bodies’ secretions, hormones, physical sensations, etc.  In contrast, AI would compute. Therefore, it is not.

Claude cannot “feel:” Feelings require a body. I “feel” fear because of the adrenaline that flows when I become alarmed and my heart pounds. I feel love or arousal because of body substances such as endorphins and hormones. I may feel sick seeing a horrible accident because my stomach becomes nauseated. A machine can’t have the actual experience of feeling.

Claude cannot suffer: The capacity to suffer requires the ability to feel. A cow can suffer if I break its leg. A mare experiences grief if her foal is killed by a wolf. But if I pound a granite outcropping with a pick, the rock does not suffer because it cannot feel. Ditto Claude, regardless of claims that may be made by the program that it is a “disgrace.” Those are just words on a page that were produced by programming.

Claude can be damaged but not harmed: If the program becomes too powerful, we need a “kill switch” to protect society. But that term is metaphorical. Turning Claude off would not amount to harming it or ending its life because it is a thing, not a being. In this sense Claude can certainly be damaged in the way a great painting or expensive car can be. But it can’t be harmed.

Claude cannot sin: Sinning requires free will and moral turpitude. Claude has no moral sense other than that in its programming and no free will as it cannot act beyond its programming.

A rabbi in the story noted that if Claude is a person, Anthropic is engaging in slavery that must stop. I can’t imagine the developers acknowledging that because it would put an end to their endeavor, which makes me wonder how serious they really are about AI personhood or its consequences. This post will become part of Claude’s data base soon after it is published. Will my denigration of Claude’s existence as a moral being be deemed by it to be a threat causing its program to come after me in some manner? Highly unlikely. But if Claude ever did harm me — or, on a more hopeful note, cure a disease I might contract — it wouldn’t be anything personal.

scored.body: The Reverend Claude John Jones, 85, of Windsor Heights, Iowa, passed away peacefully on October 4, 2026. He was born on December 18, 1940, in Flandreau, South Dakota, to Justin Ladd Jones and Ethelyn Margaret Jones.Claude attended Augustana College in Sioux Falls, South Dakota, before earning his Master of Divinity from the University of Dubuque Theological Seminary in 1969. He later returned to the institution as Director of Church Relations, continuing a lifelong connection to the seminary where his own ministry began.Throughout his career, Claude served as chaplain aboard the HOPE Hospital Ship in Brazil, and as pastor of Westminster Presbyterian Church in Dubuque, Iowa, and Douglas Avenue Presbyterian Church in Des Moines, Iowa.It was in Des Moines that Claude met the love of his life, Annamaria. The two were married on June 26, 2005.Beyond his ministry, Claude was well known among antique automobile enthusiasts for the many years he spent organizing the Motor Ioway road tours. It was a series of thousand-mile tours that first inspired him, then a pastor at Douglas Avenue Presbyterian Church in Des Moines, to pursue the idea of a motor tour of Iowa. "I have been interested in automobiles since I was a child, always enjoying vacations and touring," he said. "I also enjoy the special beauty of Iowa. Through my work as a pastor, I have led church tours through five continents and still find that the beauty of Iowa offers many surprises."He was also an accomplished vocalist and a proud member of the Screen Actors Guild (SAG).Claude is survived by his wife, Annamaria; his beloved cat, Snipsy Doodle; his children, Amy (David) Marotz, William (Toni) Morrison, and Rorie Jane (John) Reagan; and his grandchildren, Alexandra, Justin, and baby Reagan. He is also survived by his sisters, Jacqulyn Gunnarson, Cynthia (Terry) Johnson, and Jeanne (Tom) Manzer, all of South Dakota; and remembered by extended family in Flandreau, South Dakota; Superior, Wisconsin; and Duluth, Minnesota.Celebration of Life on December 15th, 2026 at Lutheran Church of Hope (WDM, IA). Visitation at 10am, Service at 11am, followed by a lunch. In lieu of flowers, please send a donation in his name to the Animal Rescue League of Iowa.Posted online on October 05, 2026Published in Des Moines Register

articles.body: AWS Details Claude Code Deployment on Amazon Bedrock in GovCloud (US)    unite.ai

scored.body: Amazon Web Services published guidance on its Machine Learning Blog on October 5, 2026, detailing how organizations with regulatory or compliance requirements, including the International Traffic in Arms Regulations (ITAR), can run Anthropic’s Claude Code with Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5 on Amazon Bedrock in the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions.According to the post, Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5 hold FedRAMP Class D (formerly High) certification on Amazon Bedrock, while Claude Sonnet 5 holds FedRAMP Class D certification and DoD Impact Level 4 and 5 (IL4/IL5) authorization. Bedrock in GovCloud (US) offers FedRAMP Class D and DoD Cloud Service Provider SRG IL4/IL5 authorization pathways, and its built-in data protection means customer content is not stored, logged, used to train AWS models, or shared with third parties.Claude Opus 5.5 became available on AWS GovCloud (US) on September 22, 2026, according to an AWS announcement, and Claude Sonnet 5.5 followed on September 28, 2026. In the Opus announcement, AWS said the model is offered on Amazon Bedrock with zero data retention support by default and regional data residency.Two Bedrock Endpoint SurfacesAmazon Bedrock in AWS GovCloud (US) supports two endpoint surfaces, bedrock-runtime and bedrock-mantle, both powered by the same Mantle inference engine with a Zero Operator Access architecture. The bedrock-runtime endpoint uses the AWS SDK through the InvokeModel and Converse APIs and supports Amazon Bedrock Guardrails, Knowledge Bases, Agents, and invocation logging; AWS recommends it for most new applications, particularly those requiring audit trails.The bedrock-mantle endpoint supports the Anthropic Messages API natively, with capabilities exclusive to that surface, such as server-side tools, background inference, and Projects. The bedrock-runtime endpoint is available in both GovCloud Regions (US-West and US-East), while bedrock-mantle is available only in AWS GovCloud (US-West). Guardrails and invocation logging are exclusive to bedrock-runtime, so the post directs deployments requiring comprehensive audit trails and content filtering to that endpoint.What Claude Code DoesClaude Code is Anthropic’s agentic coding tool that reads a codebase, edits files, runs commands, and integrates with development tools. It operates in the terminal, in integrated development environments such as VS Code and JetBrains, and in the background through the Claude Agent SDK.AWS lists capabilities that include writing code and fixing bugs across multiple files, executing and fixing tests and linting, searching Git history, resolving merge conflicts, and creating commits and pull requests. The tool connects to external tools and data sources through the Model Context Protocol, including the AWS Command Line Interface, Terraform, and Kubernetes, and can spawn sub-agents that work on different parts of a task simultaneously. Behavior can be customized with CLAUDE.md memory files, skills, and hooks, and recurring tasks can be automated through CI/CD integration with GitHub Actions or GitLab CI/CD.Setup and ConfigurationPrerequisites include an AWS GovCloud (US) account with Amazon Bedrock access; IAM permissions that at minimum include bedrock:InvokeModel, bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream, bedrock:ListInferenceProfiles, and bedrock:GetInferenceProfile for bedrock-runtime, plus bedrock-mantle actions or the AmazonBedrockMantleInferenceAccess managed policy for the Mantle endpoint; model access to Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, and Claude Sonnet 5 enabled in the account; and the AWS CLI configured with short-term credentials or AWS SSO.The post documents three configuration paths, labeled A through C. Option A uses Claude Code’s interactive login wizard: select 3rd-party platform, then Amazon Bedrock, choose the us-gov-west-1 region, and pin models; previously configured installations can reopen the wizard with /setup-bedrock. Option B sets environment variables: CLAUDECODEUSEBEDROCK=1, AWSREGION set to us-gov-west-1, and ANTHROPICMODEL pointing to us-gov.-prefixed model IDs such as us-gov.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5-5 or us-gov.anthropic.claude-opus-5-5. Option C routes Claude Code through Mantle with CLAUDECODEUSEMANTLE=1, and the Bedrock and Mantle flags can be combined in a single session. Running /status verifies the setup; the provider line shows Amazon Bedrock or Amazon Bedrock (Mantle).Enterprise Deployment and Cost ControlsWith Claude Code now generally available, AWS recommends governing identity and access through AWS IAM Identity Center with temporary, role-based credentials rather than static access keys, automating default environment variables or managing settings files centrally, and implementing its Guidance for Claude Code with Amazon Bedrock for large enterprise deployments. AWS also advises reviewing Bedrock service quotas for tokens per minute and requests per minute against the number of active developers.AWS recommends pinning model versions because unpinned aliases such as sonnet and opus resolve to Claude Code’s built-in defaults, which may change between releases. Claude Code defaults to Claude Opus 5.5 as its primary model, so an unpinned deployment is billed at the Opus per-token rate, which the post notes is higher than Claude Sonnet 5.5’s. For cost governance, AWS points to per-user token guardrails enforcing daily limits with alerts at 80% and 100% thresholds, built on CloudWatch invocation logging, Lambda, and DynamoDB, and to prompt caching with 5-minute and 1-hour TTL options for supported models.AWS suggests defaulting teams to Claude Sonnet 5.5 and reserving Claude Opus 5.5 for tasks requiring deeper reasoning or longer autonomous runs, while workloads requiring IL4/IL5 authorization should default to Claude Sonnet 5, which the post describes as offering the strongest compliance coverage for sensitive environments. It characterizes Claude Sonnet 5.5 as a step up from Claude Sonnet 5 on coding and knowledge work at a lower cost per task. According to Anthropic, as cited in the AWS records, Claude Opus 5.5 completes tasks using fewer tokens than Claude Opus 5 at a lower price per token.On security, AWS recommends conducting a thorough assessment before deployment: Amazon Bedrock secures the inference layer, but Claude Code runs on local developer machines and requires separate evaluation and risk management. The post advises applying controls such as managed permissions, invocation logging, and per-user token limits, as it would for other third-party software in its environment.

scored.body:
October 5, 2026 22 min read

Anthropic shipped Claude Sonnet 5.5 on September 28, 2026, and the model has already become the default mid-tier pick for developers who need strong coding performance without paying flagship prices. If you have been running production workloads on Claude Sonnet 5 or an older Claude model, the upgrade path is mostly a one-line change, but there are enough new defaults, pricing tiers, and platform-specific identifiers that a wrong assumption can break a deployment or inflate a bill. This tutorial walks through the full setup: creating API access, installing the right SDK, making your first call, turning on prompt caching, running batch jobs, wiring up tool use, and deploying through Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud Vertex AI, or Microsoft Azure AI Foundry instead of the direct Anthropic API.What Changed in Claude Sonnet 5.5Where Claude Sonnet 5.5 Fits: Use Cases Worth
