articles.headline: Princess Cruises Is Now Inside Claude. Here’s How to Connect It. - Joe's Daily
articles.body: Princess Cruises Is Now Inside Claude. Here’s How to Connect It.    Joe's Daily

scored.body:
Princess Cruises just became a native connector in Claude. Here's how to add it, plus the 5 tests I'd run before trusting it with a real booking.

By Joe Miragliotta

October 5, 2026

2 min read

Princess Cruises‘ PR team emailed me this morning with something I did not expect: the Princess app is now a native plugin inside Claude. Not a chatbot on their website. Inside the AI assistant itself.

Here is what that means in practice. You open Claude’s settings, head to the Connectors section, search for Princess Cruises, and add it. Then you just talk. “Find 7-day Caribbean sailings out of Fort Lauderdale” is their example, and it beats clicking through date pickers and port filters on princess.com.

The setup takes about two minutes. Sign in to Claude on a plan that supports connectors, go to Customize then Connectors then Discover, find Princess Cruises, add it, and approve the tools when it asks. In a chat, make sure the connector is switched on, then ask away. Same steps in the mobile app through the plus button.

I build AI tools for a living, so let me tell you why I am paying attention. Every travel company spent the last ten years trying to drag you into their chatbot. Princess just went the other direction and showed up where people already chat. The interface for booking travel is moving into the conversation, and a major cruise line just planted a flag there.

Testing Claude with Princess Cruises Connector

Now the honest part: I have not put it through its paces yet. Before I trust it with real money, here is my test list.

The basic search: does it return real sailings with dates and ships, or vague suggestions?

The price check: are the fares it quotes the same ones on princess.com?

The comparison: ask for the cheapest balcony in January and see if it can actually reason across options.

The handoff: when I say book it, where do I land?

The fine print: ask what is not included and see if it tells the truth.

I am running those this week. If you beat me to it, tell me what it got wrong. I have got the line’s whole fleet ranked by age here if you want to know which ship you would end up on.

The Find Newsletter

The good stuff, all in one place. Every week, we round up products worth buying, places worth going, and travel finds worth knowing about, all handpicked by Joe’s Daily.

One email a week. No spam, no list-selling, unsubscribe in a click.

articles.body: Pixel Search could soon get a Gemini-powered upgrade along with privacy improvements    Android Authority

scored.body:
Joe Maring / Android AuthorityAdd Android Authority on Google: TL;DR

The latest Pixel Search update adds a new “Privacy & Permissions” section in the Pixel Search app’s settings.

It lets users choose whether they want the app to use their call logs and SMS history to improve contact suggestions.

We also spotted evidence that a new “Gemini-powered suggestions” feature could be introduced in the Pixel Search app.

The new Pixel Search app that comes preloaded on the Pixel 11 series makes the app drawer more useful than ever before. It lets users search for photos, emails, contacts, and more. Now, it seems Google is prepping to give the app a Gemini-powered upgrade while also giving users more control over their call logs and message data in Pixel Search.You’re reading an Authority Insights story. Authority Insights brings you all the latest exclusive reports, app teardowns, leaks, and in-depth tech coverage from the Android Authority team that you won’t find anywhere else.The latest version of the app (1.0.983036833) introduces a new “Privacy & Permissions” section in its settings. It includes three toggles: “Help improve Pixel Search,” “Call Logs,” and “SMS.”Users can disable the “Help improve Pixel Search” toggle if they don’t want their data to be aggregated and used for usage insights. Similarly, the “Call Logs” and “SMS” toggles can be turned off if you don’t want Google to use your call and SMS history to improve contact suggestions in Pixel Search.It’s worth noting that disabling the “Call Logs” or “SMS” toggle doesn’t prevent Pixel Search from surfacing results from your call history or messages. Users can stop their call logs or messages from appearing in search results altogether by revoking the “Call logs” and “SMS” permissions on the app’s “App Permissions” page.AssembleDebug / Android AuthorityWe also dug through the app’s code and found evidence of an upcoming feature called “Gemini-powered suggestions.” Based on the strings we found, this feature will proactively surface relevant information and actions to help users complete tasks faster.Here are the strings that we found in the Pixel Search app’s code:Code<string name="search_setting_gemini_suggestions_title">Show Gemini-powered suggestions</string>

<string name="search_setting_gemini_suggestions_summary">See relevant info and Gemini-suggested actions to help you finish a task faster</string>Gemini-powered suggestions don’t seem to be available yet, but they could roll out in a future update. However, the new “Privacy & Permissions” section is already available in the latest version of Pixel Search.You can update the Pixel Search app on your Pixel 11 via the Play Store. If you’re using an older Pixel, you can sideload and use the app as long as your device is running Android 17 QPR2 Beta 5 or newer.⚠️ An APK teardown helps predict features that may arrive on a service in the future based on work-in-progress code. However, it is possible that such predicted features may not make it to a public release.FollowThank you for being part of our community. Read our Comment Policy before posting.

articles.headline: ChatGPT, Gemini and Google never name 9 of 40 UK software firms in shortlists - PPC Land
articles.body: ChatGPT, Gemini and Google never name 9 of 40 UK software firms in shortlists    PPC Land

scored.body:
Nine of 40 UK B2B software companies were named in none of the 24 shortlist answers they received from four AI platforms, according to The AI Shortlist 2026, a report Recrawled published on September 29, 2026. The same research reports YouTube in 25% of Google AI Overview answers about the companies and in none of the 360 ChatGPT answers.In ShortA UK agency put 1,608 questions of the kind software buyers type to ChatGPT, Gemini and two Google search tools, then checked which British software companies came back in the answers. Nine of the 40 companies it studied closely were never recommended on any of the four tools when a buyer asked who to consider, even though every one of the 40 was recognised once its name was typed in. So a company's place in an AI answer depends on how the question is worded and which tool is asked, and the results describe one day, September 4, 2026, rather than a permanent ranking.A one-day snapshot of 1,608 questionsRecrawled describes itself as an answer engine optimisation (AEO) agency, and The AI Shortlist 2026 was researched by two of its co-founders, Jess Brookes and Charles Törnros. The study began with 200 UK-headquartered B2B software companies, each with between 20 and 150 staff and selling a specialist product to other organisations. They were spread across seven sectors: contact centre and customer experience, HR and workforce, compliance and risk, fintech and insurtech, supply chain and field service, healthtech and edtech, and other specialist software. According to the report, each company was checked against its own website, its filings and its review-site listings rather than pulled from a list. Forty were then studied in depth, in 33 buyer categories across six of the seven sectors.The questions went to ChatGPT, Gemini, Google AI Overviews and Google AI Mode, each in default mode, signed out and with the location set to the UK. The run took place on September 4, 2026. In all, 1,608 questions were put: 168 to the sectors (six broad questions per sector, on each of four platforms) and 1,440 about the 40 companies. Every studied company received nine questions, six asking which companies to shortlist and three asking about the company by name. On four platforms that comes to 36 answers per company, 24 to the shortlist questions and 12 to the by-name ones. Of the 1,608 questions, 1,600 produced answers. The remaining eight were by-name questions for which Google displayed no AI Overview, and the report records that outcome as a result in its own right.The six shortlist questions covered different buying situations. Three say UK or name a UK buyer. One drops the country and names the size of the buyer instead, one starts from the market leader's name, and one is a head-to-head between the leader and its nearest rival. In the report's example, the UK-specific wording asks about court bundling software for a UK law firm, while the size-based version asks about court bundling software for mid-sized law firms.Recognised, but not recommendedThe executive summary carries its argument in a heading: "Being recognised by AI is not the same as making the shortlist." When checked by name, all 40 companies were correctly identified by at least one platform, according to Recrawled. Asking which companies to consider produced a different picture. Twenty-nine were named on at least one shortlist question that specified the UK, two were named only when the question did not say UK, and nine were named in none of their 24 shortlist answers, on any platform. No company appeared in all 24. The most any managed was 22.Wording changed the resultFour of the six shortlist questions tested the same companies in different buying situations. A company counts in the report's chart if any of the four platforms named it anywhere in the answer; the final column is the appendix's count of individual answers.

Question typeCompanies named by at least one platformIndividual answers naming the companyUK-specific shortlist question63% (25 of 40)36% (173 of 480)Mid-sized buyer, no "UK"43% (17 of 40)22% (35 of 160)Alternatives to the market leader13% (5 of 39)4% (6 of 156)Market leader against nearest rival0% (0 of 38)0% (0 of 152)

One company was excluded from the alternatives question and two from the head-to-head question because their own product was the subject. For the same reason the answer-level figures add up to 948 rather than 960: 12 answers in which a company's own product was the subject are left out. The company was named in 11 of those 12, so across all 960 answers it was named 225 times, or 23%.The first two question types were equally specific, according to the report, so the drop was not simply the result of narrower wording. In one category, removing "UK" was enough for three of the four platforms to switch to companies based outside the UK. A buyer asking for alternatives to the market leader is "explicitly looking beyond the market leader", yet only 13% of the companies studied appeared in those answers. The fourth question set the market leader versus its nearest rival. None of the other 38 companies showed up in any of the four platform answers, according to Recrawled; AI sometimes introduced another brand, just never one of the companies studied. Because that prompt already names two vendors, the result measures whether a third name found room in the answer, which is narrower than general invisibility.The platforms disagreedOf the 31 companies named on at least one platform, Gemini never named 13 (42%), Google AI Mode 11 (35%), Google AI Overviews six (19%) and ChatGPT five (16%). Across the same 240 shortlist questions, Google AI Overviews named the studied companies 69 times and AI Mode 44. Google's two AI experiences therefore differed substantially from each other, according to the report.Other datasets point toward platform divergence as well. The Semrush AI Visibility Index, covered by PPC Land on June 30, 2026, analysed 126 million US prompts from January to April 2026 and found that only 36 of more than 1,200 brands kept top-100 status on every platform in every month studied. In that index the mention-source overlap, which Semrush reports by platform, was 64% on AI Overviews and 30% on Gemini, and the average number of brands named per response ran from 3.3 on ChatGPT to 5.2 on AI Mode.Video citations separate Google from the other platformsAccording to the report, YouTube appeared in 25% of Google AI Overview answers and 19% of AI Mode answers about the 40 companies. For Gemini the share was 2%, and ChatGPT showed none in its 360 answers. The wording shifts within the document, though: pages 5 and 10 say YouTube "appeared", while the appendix says the answers "cited at least one video". Counted by citations rather than answers, YouTube was 3.3% of the 7,704 citations across every answer the researchers read, and by distinct pages it was 4% of 2,750 pages on 1,223 websites.Measurements elsewhere differ by platform, market and method. Meltwater's analysis for August 2026, reported by PPC Land on September 23, tracked eight systems including ChatGPT and ranked YouTube the most-cited platform across all eight. Recrawled's zero for ChatGPT sits apart from that finding. The datasets differ in query type, market, period and measure, and the report does not address Meltwater's work. Tinuiti's Q2 2026 report, in the same article, found that YouTube citations in AI Mode more than quadrupled between January and April 2026, and in AI Overviews more than doubled.Cited, but not recommendedEight of the 40 companies had their own pages cited in answers that recommended somebody else, across 19 answers, according to the report. One vendor selling software that checks suppliers' security had published a guide to the best software in its category. AI cited the guide in nine shortlist answers. In four of them, it used the vendor's content but recommended other companies. In the report's usage, cited means the answer displayed the page as one of its sources, while named means the company itself appeared in the answer.The report's source breakdown shows where the cited material came from. Of the 2,750 distinct pages, 67% were on software vendors' own websites, 9% on review directories, 4% on YouTube, 3% on official and industry bodies, 3% on press, blogs and forums, and 14% on other sites. Pages were classified by website, with vendor sites matched against every brand named in the run and a random 100 read by hand as a check. Around a quarter of the pages cited in each company's shortlist answers sat on the websites of the most frequently named companies in its category.A separate study points at a similar gap between being cited and being chosen. Scrunch, which sells AI visibility monitoring, analysed roughly 10,000 AI-cited URLs and found that when a brand's own ranked list was cited, the brand's recommendation rate rose from about 4% to roughly 7%, and its mention rate from about 19% to 39%. A competitor was recommended instead of the author 24.3% of the time. PPC Land reported the study, which covered data collected from May 17 to June 30, 2026, in late September.Review counts did not track namingAcross the 40 companies, the correlation between review volume and AI naming was -0.06, which the report calls effectively zero. The company named most often had 19 Capterra reviews and no G2 listing, and it appeared in 22 of its 24 answers. One company with 637 reviews was named in just one of 24. Among the ten companies named most, the typical company had two to three reviews across G2 and Capterra; among the nine never named, the typical company had 13. Counts were taken from G2 and Capterra on the day of the run, and a missing listing counted as zero.The report is careful about what this does and does not show. Finding no link, it says, is "not proof there is no link anywhere". Among the companies named most, Recrawled says it repeatedly saw specific third-party proof and measurable facts in the answers and pages that named them, which it describes as "an observed pattern, not evidence that those signals caused the naming".Buyer behaviour gives some context. A Semrush survey of 519 B2B buyers who use AI tools for work, published by PPC Land on July 20, 2026, found that 92% said AI had shaped their vendor shortlist and 66% had spotted vendors missing from AI answers. Only 7% said brand recognition determines whether they notice a vendor in AI responses, against 53% who prioritise a close match with their specific use case. And 38% checked reviews on G2 or similar sites after receiving an AI recommendation.Dominant brands, and room beneath themOf the 33 buyer categories, 61% had one dominant brand appearing in at least three-quarters of the answers. Even so, 50% of the 40 companies took first position on at least one buyer question. Each category received the same six shortlist questions on four platforms, so 24 answers, read once for each company in it.The limit of a strong position shows in one example. A vendor that was not the leader in its category was named in 16 of its 24 answers, on all four platforms, in much the same terms each time. When the buyer asked for alternatives to the leader, or compared the leader with its nearest rival, it was named in none of those eight answers.The appendix adds a wider view. On the six broad sector questions, separate from the shortlist set, 23 of the 200 companies were named at all, and global brands dominated. Contact centre and customer experience software returned 54 different brand names, one of them in 17 of that sector's 24 answers; fintech and insurtech returned 98.Accuracy once the buyer knows the nameThe sixth finding moves from visibility to correctness. Of the 40 companies checked by name on four platforms, one in three got at least one answer about the wrong business, two in five had review questions answered using employee-review sites, and one in five had pricing come back inconsistently or without a source. Thirteen of the 40 shared a name with an unrelated business or product.The report lists four examples:A UK desk-booking vendor was answered as a restaurant and cocktail bar in Northampton, by ChatGPT.A UK contact-centre vendor was answered as a Continental car tyre, by Gemini and Google AI Overviews.A UK insurance-data vendor was answered as a Dyson robot vacuum cleaner, by Gemini and Google AI Mode.A UK cyber-risk vendor was answered as a cannabis producer, by Gemini.The employee-review problem has a quotable case. Google AI Mode reproduced an employee-review site verbatim in response to a reviews question for one vendor: "Was a great company, on the decline." Elsewhere in its answers, according to the report, AI Mode had called that vendor's product "the gold standard".Same-name confusion has appeared outside B2B software. In July 2026, a Google AI Overview told searchers that Anna Mae's Bakery and Restaurant in Millbank, Ontario was closing on July 31; the closure belonged to a different business of the same name in Illinois.Why the findings matter to marketing teamsThe report opens with three figures from other organisations. According to 6sense's 2025 B2B Buyer Experience Report, covering nearly 4,000 buyers, 95% of purchases went to a vendor already on the buyer's Day One shortlist. Forrester's 2026 report The State Of Business Buying, with nearly 18,000 buyers, found that 94% of business buyers used AI while buying. TrustRadius, in its 2026 B2B Buying Disconnect Report of 1,862 buyers, found that 83% of technology buyers shortlisted three or fewer products, with an average shortlist of 2.7. Recrawled's framing is that the list is short, forms early, and now passes in part through AI.Other numbers point the same way. Bain data cited in a LinkedIn marketing blog post, and covered by PPC Land on May 26, 2026, put the share of B2B buyers who start with a day-one vendor list at 86%, with 81% buying from it. Whether marketing teams can see their position on that list is a separate question. An index from Agentcy found that 81% of 104 senior B2B marketing leaders consider AI visibility a blind spot and that only 10% can consistently connect AI-driven touchpoints to revenue. PPC Land reported it on March 5, 2026.Software vendors have started to build measurement for the gap. HubSpot's AEO tool, reported on April 14, 2026, tracks brand visibility in ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity and costs $50 a month as a standalone product. Cloudflare opened an AEO Visibility Dashboard in early access on August 6, 2026, covering Claude and GPT models. Recrawled's study differs in form: one fixed day, a defined sample, and separate counts per question type and per platform, which the report argues a single blended score would hide.Recrawled's recommendations and commercial positionEach finding in the report ends with a recommendation box. Recrawled recommends building visibility around the buying situations that matter rather than one broad category question, and tracking platforms separately instead of as a blended score. It also recommends content that shows why a company belongs on the shortlist for the problems it solves, specific proof rather than review volume as the goal, consistent category, pricing and product claims across sources, and a focus on the situations where a company has the strongest reason to win.The authors also sell services in this area. According to the report, Recrawled offers diagnosis and setup, repair and optimisation, and management and continuity, plus a free AI Shortlist Assessment covering ChatGPT, Gemini, Google AI Overviews, Google AI Mode and Claude, delivered by email within three working days. The companies studied were not contacted and took no part in the research, according to the report.What the data does not showThe report states its limits. It is "a snapshot of one day", and 40 companies are "a sample, not a census". Recrawled notes that the same questions asked the next day may produce different answers on all four platforms, and that nothing in the study predicts what any platform will say next. SISTRIX's 17-week measurement across three platforms and six countries gives a sense of the movement involved: AI Mode rotated 56% of its citations each week and ChatGPT 74%, while AI Overviews stayed completely stable for just over half of queries, according to the analysis PPC Land reported on April 30, 2026.Recrawled also separates citation from cause. The platforms report which pages they cited, not why they named the companies they named, so a cited page is an observation and not an explanation of a recommendation.Two presentation points stand out in the document itself. The executive summary counts 29 companies named on at least one UK-specific shortlist question, while the first bar in the wording chart shows 25 for the UK-specific question type, and the report does not set out the four-company difference in so many words. The YouTube figure is described as appearance in one place and as citing at least one video in another. Neither changes the headline count of nine companies named in none of their 24 shortlist answers, but both leave open exactly which answers each percentage covers. Fuller methodology is available from Recrawled on request, according to the report.TimelineMarch 5, 2026 - Agentcy index finds 81% of 104 senior B2B marketing leaders call AI visibility a blind spot.April 14, 2026 - HubSpot adds a standalone AEO tool tracking ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity.April 30, 2026 - SISTRIX 17-week analysis is reported, showing AI Mode rotating 56% of citations weekly and ChatGPT 74%.May 26, 2026 - Bain figures on day-one vendor lists are reported: 86% of B2B buyers start with one, 81% buy from it.June 30, 2026 - Semrush AI Visibility Index shows 36 of more than 1,200 brands holding top-100 status on every platform.July 18-19, 2026 - An AI Overview wrongly says an Ontario bakery is closing on July 31.July 20, 2026 - Semrush B2B buyer survey results are published: 92% say AI shaped their vendor shortlist.August 6, 2026 - Cloudflare opens its AEO Visibility Dashboard in early access.September 4, 2026 - Recrawled puts 1,608 questions to ChatGPT, Gemini, Google AI Overviews and Google AI Mode.September 23, 2026 - Meltwater and Tinuiti YouTube citation data is reported.September 24, 2026 - Scrunch study on self-ranked lists and AI recommendations is reported.September 29, 2026 - Recrawled publishes The AI Shortlist 2026.Semrush: 36 brands win AI visibility everywhere, 1,200 vanish on one - Semrush's index of 126 million US prompts compares brand visibility across AI platforms from January to April 2026.Brand recognition sways just 7% of B2B AI buyers, Semrush finds - a survey of 519 B2B buyers on how AI shapes vendor shortlists and what they check afterwards.Self-ranked brands gain AI recommendations from 4% to 7%, Scrunch finds - an analysis of roughly 10,000 AI-cited URLs on what happens when a brand's own list is cited.Google switched on AI Mode checkout for Shopify stores without asking - an article that also carries Meltwater and Tinuiti data on YouTube citations across AI systems.SISTRIX April 2026: AI citation drift and the death of keyword research - a 17-week measurement of how much AI citations change from week to week.Google AI Overview forces Anna Mae's Bakery to deny fake July 31 closing - a case of an AI Overview confusing two same-name businesses.LinkedIn's three-phase B2B launch framework: why one day is not enough - includes Bain figures on day-one vendor lists and purchases.Most B2B marketers can't prove AI's role in their pipeline - Agentcy's index of 104 senior B2B marketing leaders on AI visibility and revenue attribution.HubSpot launches AEO tool as organic traffic drops 27% for its customers - details of HubSpot's AI visibility tracker and its pricing.Cloudflare scores brand visibility inside Claude and GPT answers - Cloudflare's early-access dashboard for citation rate, mention rate and share of voice.SummaryWho: Recrawled, a UK answer engine optimisation agency, through its co-founders Jess Brookes and Charles Törnros. The subjects were 200 UK-headquartered B2B software companies with 20 to 150 staff, of which 40 were studied in depth. The platforms queried were ChatGPT, Gemini, Google AI Overviews and Google AI Mode.What: A report titled The AI Shortlist 2026, based on 1,608 questions and 1,600 answers. Nine of the 40 companies were named in none of their 24 shortlist answers. Named share fell from 63% to 43% to 13% to 0% as the question moved from a UK-specific shortlist to a no-country version, to alternatives to the leader, to a leader-versus-rival comparison. YouTube appeared in 25% of AI Overview answers and none of ChatGPT's 360, and review volume showed a correlation of -0.06 with naming.When: The research was run on September 4, 2026 and published on September 29, 2026.Where: The questions were asked with each platform in default mode, signed out and with the location set to the UK, about UK B2B software companies.Why: Recrawled set out to learn what gets a B2B software company into an AI shortlist, citing figures that buyers form short lists early and increasingly use AI. The report's authors sell AEO services, and the study is a one-day sample of 40 companies, which Recrawled itself describes as not a census.

articles.headline: Google Gemini cited in $69K crypto scam report - Cryptonews.net
articles.body: Google Gemini cited in $69K crypto scam report    Cryptonews.net

scored.body:
Google Gemini has been cited in a crypto investigator’s report alleging that Tronify.rent took $69,651 from roughly 80 victims during September after at least one user said the AI service had described the website as safe.

JP, founder of IOC Investigations, said the TRON-focused website received funds from victims through several addresses and claimed a victim had asked Gemini whether the service was legitimate before interacting with it. His Oct. 4 post listed 12 TRON addresses that he associated with the operation.

SOMEHOW, this scammer was able to get Google’s Gemini to recommend his fake website and steal $69,651 – IN ONE MONTH!About 80 people fell victim to Tronify dot rent last month. According to a victim report, Gemini even confirmed that it was a safe website!That is insane!… pic.twitter.com/A9hyayOhFU

— JP (@rugpullfinder) October 4, 2026

Know when yourcoins moveAlerts, real-time prices, and market news — all in one app

4.8 based on 40K reviews in the App Store and Google Play

The $69,651 figure and roughly 80-victim count come from JP’s investigation. No independent blockchain-forensics report reviewed for this article has separately reproduced the full loss total across the listed addresses.

Tronify scam claims center on wallet connections

Tronify.rent presents itself as a TRON energy rental service promising to cut transaction costs for users moving assets on the network.

The website currently claims it is a noncustodial service and tells visitors they retain control of their assets. Its interface includes a wallet connection feature and promotes energy delegation for TRC-20 transactions.

Victim reports tell a different story. A Reddit user reported in June that funds were drained after connecting a Trust Wallet to Tronify.rent, claiming a loss of 2,590 USDT. The account said it later filed a complaint with the FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center. Reddit posts are user-generated reports and do not independently establish criminal liability.

JP’s October post said approximately 80 people were affected during the previous month. He published the addresses he linked to the activity but did not provide a public transaction-by-transaction breakdown showing how the $69,651 total was calculated.

The investigator separately flagged tron.store as another suspected scam site. Independent threat research provides some support for concern around related infrastructure: PhishDestroy previously recorded a domain using the page title “tron.store – Rent Energy” and classified the associated site as high risk for crypto phishing and brand impersonation.

Independent security checks flagged Tronify months earlier

Security warnings about Tronify.rent predate the latest victim report. PhishDestroy flagged the domain in February and later assigned it a critical threat rating of 90/100. Its stored intelligence identified crypto-scam and brand-impersonation signals and recorded threat-feed detections tied to the site.

The security service recorded two abuse reports in April, including one sent to the domain registrar and another escalation that copied ICANN Compliance. Its monitoring later found the domain remained reachable. PhishDestroy cautions that an outgoing abuse report does not prove a registrar received, investigated or acted on the complaint.

WHOIS records show that Tronify.rent was registered on Nov. 25, 2025, with registrant details hidden through a privacy service. The registration currently lists TLD Registrar Solutions as the registrar.

The website itself claims to operate as “Tronify Energy Solutions LLC,” lists a Florida address and says its infrastructure is SOC 2 Type II compliant. No independent audit or regulatory document confirming those website claims was identified in the sources reviewed for this report.

JP claimed the operation used DDoS protection linked to Russia. Independent network data reviewed here does not confirm that point. PhishDestroy’s stored observations identified Cloudflare as the site’s edge network and noted that the origin server was hidden behind the CDN, meaning the origin’s geographic location could not be established from that edge IP.

Gemini recommendation claim remains unconfirmed by Google

The most unusual part of the report concerns Google Gemini. JP said a victim reported asking Gemini whether Tronify.rent was safe and receiving a response that appeared to endorse the website. The investigator described the reported answer as Gemini confirming the site was safe.

No public statement from Google reviewed for this article has confirmed that interaction, identified the prompt used or explained how Gemini may have evaluated the website.

Google nevertheless explicitly warns that generative AI can produce inaccurate information and tells users to check claims presented as facts using other sources.

Its general Gemini guidance similarly says Gemini Apps can make mistakes and advises users to double-check responses before relying on them.

Google’s AI security documentation goes further when web content is involved. The company explains that malicious webpages can contain material intended to influence generative AI systems through prompt-injection techniques. Google says Gemini uses safeguards to detect suspicious material, though users can still report responses they believe are unsafe or inaccurate.

Google has separately warned about cryptocurrency fraud using artificial intelligence. In a June fraud advisory, the company reported scams involving fake crypto investments, fraudulent mining software and deceptive AI bot tutorials designed to lead users toward malicious code or wallet-draining activity.

AI is becoming part of crypto scam tactics

The Tronify allegation comes as security researchers continue documenting scams that use AI branding or trusted technology platforms to make malicious offers appear safer.

In September, TRM Labs documented fake AI trading bot tutorials that stole $517,000 from 224 victims. The campaign used videos presenting automated crypto-arbitrage tools while malicious infrastructure caused users to deploy contracts that sent funds to attacker-controlled addresses.

Another campaign used Google-style phishing emails targeting crypto traders, relying on legitimate-looking Google account notifications to make malicious links appear more trustworthy.

The mechanism described in the Tronify complaints resembles the risks covered in crypto.news’ guide to wallet drainers and approval phishing, where users authorize transactions or permissions that later allow attackers to move tokens from their wallets.

Independent threat data on Tronify.rent shows why an AI-generated safety answer, if the victim report is accurate, would have conflicted with existing warning signs. By April, the domain had already been reported to its registrar by a security service, while later scans continued to classify it as high risk.

Google’s current Gemini safety guidance says users should evaluate AI-generated responses critically and verify claims before acting, especially where inaccurate information could create financial or security risks.

articles.headline: Open Source Mod Brings Rate Limits, Costs and CI Status Into View for Claude Code Users - DevOps.com
articles.body: Open Source Mod Brings Rate Limits, Costs and CI Status Into View for Claude Code Users    DevOps.com

scored.body:
TL;DR — Key Takeaways

Claude Statuspane adds a floating dashboard to Claude Code showing context consumption, five-hour and seven-day limits, session cost, model settings and Git information.

GitHub Actions integration and a simple progress API let developers see CI results and background task status without leaving the terminal.

The open-source project is useful at the individual level, but DevOps teams ultimately need centralized, auditable telemetry covering agent spend, limits and pipeline outcomes.

AI coding agents burn through resources in ways that are hard to see. A developer starts a long task in Claude Code, and the session quietly eats into a context window, a five-hour rate limit, a weekly cap, and a budget. Most of the time, nobody notices until something runs out.An open-source project called Claude Statuspane takes a crack at that problem. Built by developer Anji Xu and published on GitHub under an MIT license, it adds a floating status card above the Claude Code prompt in the terminal. The card shows the active model and reasoning effort level, how much of the context window is in use, progress against five-hour and seven-day rate limits with reset countdowns, the current directory and git branch, and the session’s running cost.It’s a small tool. But it points to a bigger issue for DevOps teams. As AI agents take on longer, more autonomous work, the people running them need the same kind of telemetry they already expect from build systems and production services.Claude Code already supports a statusLine setting that runs a shell script and prints a single line of text. Statuspane goes further by using Claude Code’s new mod system, which lets plugins draw interface elements inside a terminal session. That system is still in early access, and the project’s README warns that the API may change between Claude Code releases.Instead of plain text, the card uses gauges. A context bar might show 42%, or 222,000 of 1 million tokens. Bars shift to a warning color at 60% and an error color at 85%. A compact button sits next to the context gauge, so a developer can trigger /compact before a session hits its limit. The card follows Claude Code’s themes and collapses to a single button when it’s in the way. It requires Claude Code 2.1.287 or later and a terminal at least 70 columns wide. It doesn’t run in the Claude Code desktop app, which has its own status display.The most useful feature for DevOps teams may be the GitHub CI integration. With the GitHub CLI signed in, the card can show the latest GitHub Actions run for the current branch. It checks every minute, and every 10 seconds while a run is active. A second option tracks runs triggered by a git push or gh pr merge and keeps them on screen for 10 minutes after they finish. The card shows whether a job is running, failed, or deployed, and how long ago.That closes a loop that agents often leave open. An agent pushes a change, and the developer switches to a browser tab to see whether the pipeline passed. Putting build status beside the prompt keeps the human and the agent looking at the same result.Statuspane also includes a simple progress API. Any script can write a small JSON file to a progress folder with a label, a percentage, a short text field, a time-to-live, and a state of running, ok, or error. The card watches the 20 most recently written files and refreshes every second. Rows disappear when their TTL expires, so stale jobs don’t pile up. Shell and Python helpers are included, and other mods can call the API directly.The author also built in some sensible guardrails. The progress folder accepts only JSON files up to 64 KB, and it strips control characters, bidirectional marks, and zero-width characters from text fields. That matters. Anything that renders text inside an agent’s terminal is a possible path for injected content. Everything runs locally, and CI lookups use the developer’s own GitHub CLI credentials rather than a third-party service.The project is brand new, has little adoption so far, and depends on an early-access API that a Claude Code update could break. Teams should treat it as an experiment.But the idea behind it is sound. Usage-based limits and token costs are now part of daily developer work. A team that can’t see per-session costs can’t manage them. And as agents run longer jobs on their own, the human in the loop needs a quick way to see what’s happening without digging through logs.Still, one developer’s view only goes so far. “Statuspane gives one developer a gauge, which is useful and stops short of governance,” said Mitch Ashley, vice president and practice lead for CIO & Technology Buyers and Software Lifecycle Engineering at The Futurum Group. “Agent deployment pace is set by what an organization can observe, control, and prove, and a personal status card shows a team none of those.”Ashley said the real measure lies elsewhere. “The test is whether spend, limits, and pipeline outcomes per agent session can be collected centrally and audited. Watch whether agent platforms ship that telemetry natively.”Expect more tools like this as coding agents become extensible platforms. Statuspane solves a real problem for the person at the keyboard. The bigger job for DevOps and platform teams is getting the same data into shared systems, where every agent session’s spend, limits, and pipeline results can be tracked and reviewed. Until agent platforms provide that, a personal status card is a useful start, not the finish line.

Frequently Asked QuestionsWhat is Claude Statuspane?Claude Statuspane is an open-source Claude Code mod created by Anji Xu that displays usage, context, cost, Git and CI information in a floating terminal card.What does Statuspane monitor?It can show the active model, reasoning effort, context-window usage, five-hour and seven-day rate limits, reset countdowns, session cost, Git branch information and recent GitHub Actions activity.Is Statuspane an enterprise AI governance tool?No. It gives individual developers useful visibility, but enterprise teams still need centralized systems capable of collecting, auditing and governing spend, limits and pipeline outcomes across agent sessions.

members.title: Prototyping Game Cutscenes With Veo 3.1 - criticalhit.net

representative.headline: Prototyping Game Cutscenes With Veo 3.1 - criticalhit.net

articles.headline: Prototyping Game Cutscenes With Veo 3.1 - criticalhit.net
articles.body: Prototyping Game Cutscenes With Veo 3.1    criticalhit.net

scored.body:
A cutscene can look good on paper and still drag when somebody watches it. Perhaps the pilot explains too much. Perhaps the camera reveals the threat before the character notices it. Those are useful problems to find while the scene is still a handful of shots, before a team has built the cockpit or rigged its occupant.

Storyboards and animatics give developers that chance. An animatic is a rough edit used to test a scene’s timing. For a small team without much time for drawing, AI video offers another way to put one together.

Google’s Veo 3.1 generates audio alongside video, including dialogue and background sound. That makes it worth considering for cutscene planning: you can hear where a line sits against the action, then decide whether the scene deserves further work.

What Veo 3.1 gives you to work with

Check the settings in the service you plan to use. Veo 3.1 supports text prompts, image-led generation and first-and-last-frame control, but the available combinations depend on the model and interface.

Google’s Gemini API documentation lists four-, six- and eight-second generation, with eight seconds required for 1080p and 4K output. Lite supports up to 1080p. Both landscape 16:9 and portrait 9:16 are available. Reference-image support has its own restrictions, so don’t assume every setting works with every input.

For a first animatic, try allocating the shots this way:

Standard: dialogue close-ups and moments where the expression matters.

Fast: chase sequences, vehicles and other shots you expect to revise repeatedly.

Lite: establishing views, backgrounds and early mood tests.

That’s a sensible starting plan, not a finding from a controlled comparison. Run one representative shot before committing the whole sequence to a tier.

Eight seconds won’t hold a long conversation. It can, however, hold a glance at a warning light or a brief exchange before a cut. Build around those smaller beats.

Three jobs it handles well

The dialogue beat

Put the spoken line in quotation marks and describe the delivery. Is the character frightened, trying to hide it, or simply tired? Add the background sound separately so the request is easy to follow.

Then listen to the result without looking at the picture. Does the line explain something the audience already knows? Is there room for a reaction? A temporary performance can help you ask those questions earlier, though its delivery shouldn’t be mistaken for the best an actor could bring to the scene.

If the voice is distracting, replace it with a scratch recording in the edit. You still have something useful to cut against.

The action shot

A vehicle chase gives you several decisions to test. Where does the camera sit? Can the viewer tell which way the car is moving? Is the obstacle visible before the driver reacts?

Start with one maneuver, such as a turn into a narrow tunnel. Watch for impossible movement or a road that changes shape. An attractive clip can hide poor spatial continuity. For a game introduction, the useful result is a shot that makes the route and the danger clear.

The tone test

Keep the action and framing similar, then change the treatment. Try a worn industrial setting, a brightly colored miniature world or a clay-like stop-motion look.

Compare what each version does for the story. A handmade style might make an otherwise bleak exchange feel funny. A realistic treatment might make the same line seem too theatrical. These are decisions you can explore before commissioning finished art.

A sample prompt for a cutscene beat

Keep the request to one short beat. Describe the framing, character and action, then add lighting and sound. For example:

Medium close-up, slow dolly in. A tired salvage pilot in her forties with a shaved head and a scratched orange flight suit sits in a cramped cockpit lit by flickering amber warning lights. She taps a cracked display, exhales, and says flatly: "Fuel for one jump. Make it count." Rain of sparks behind the canopy glass, 35mm lens, heavy film grain. Sound: alarm chime, creaking hull, low engine hum. No subtitles.

Treat "No subtitles" as an instruction to the model, not a guarantee. Check the returned footage for unwanted text. And if the pilot rushes through the line, simplify the action before adding more directions to the prompt.

Building a sequence from single shots

An animatic needs an edit. Several impressive clips sitting in a folder won’t tell you whether the scene works.

Write a shot list with one main action per shot. Add what the audience needs to learn from it.

Generate a rough version of each shot, using the tier choices above as a starting point.

Use your own concept art as a start image if it already exists. Text prompts are enough to begin when it doesn’t.

Carry a usable end frame into the next shot where that helps continuity. For a new camera angle, check the eyeline and screen direction yourself.

Assemble the clips with temporary sound. Trim them freely; you don’t have to use every generated second.

Watch the whole scene, note where attention drops and revise the shot list.

Before generating, compare the current options on PixelDojo, which publishes example prompts and tier prices. Its listed eight-second 1080p clips cost 96 credits on Standard with audio, 36 on Fast with audio and 16 on Lite. Example tiles can show sale prices, so check the generation screen for the actual charge.

Budget for retries as well as the first attempt. A cheap shot that needs six attempts can cost more than the one you accept immediately.

Where it falls short, and the rules to follow

Check continuity across every cut. Faces, clothing and props may change between generations; reference images can help, but you still need to inspect the sequence. Look closely at hands, small text and interactions between characters.

The result is also a video, not an editable game scene. It won’t give you a rig, a camera track or a playable level. Once the timing feels right, test essential staging in a rough engine scene, especially where the cinematic hands control back to the player.

Use original characters and reference material you have permission to upload. Before carrying generated footage into a release, review the service terms and the destination’s current requirements. Steam’s Content Survey focuses its AI disclosure on generated content shipped with the game and consumed by players, distinguishing that from tools used for efficiency behind the scenes.

The useful question at the end of the animatic is simple: what should the team build? If the edit tells you to drop two shots and shorten the pilot’s speech, it has already done a worthwhile job.

Last Updated: October 5, 2026

articles.headline: Google's Bold Gemini 4 Argon Leads 14 of 19 AI Benchmarks - Parametric Architecture
articles.body: Google's Bold Gemini 4 Argon Leads 14 of 19 AI Benchmarks    Parametric Architecture

scored.body:
Google has introduced Gemini 4 Argon, its most capable model to date. Early results show it leading or matching the strongest competitors on most of the tests the company chose to highlight.

Official visual for the launch of Google’s Gemini 4 Argon model. Image credit: News from Google

According to Google’s published comparisons, Argon beats or ties GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 on 14 of 19 benchmarks. The clearest advantages appear in professional knowledge work: multi-step financial research, legal research and drafting, and end-to-end business automation. Coding results are more mixed. Argon sets a new high mark on DeepSWE v1.1, a long-horizon software-engineering suite, yet trails on certain terminal and systems-level tests. The model can generate responses up to one million tokens long, giving it unusual room for extended reasoning and document handling.

- Advertisement -

For the moment access is tightly controlled. Trusted testers and cybersecurity teams have early entry. Paid API customers and Google AI Ultra subscribers are expected to follow.

Where Argon pulls ahead

The strongest signals come from tasks that resemble real professional workflows rather than pure academic puzzles. On AutomationBench, which measures a model’s ability to complete multi-step business processes, Argon scores 51.3 percent, several points clear of the next-best systems. On Vals Finance Agent v2 it reaches 65.4 percent.

On Harvey’s Legal Agent Benchmark the margin is even larger, with Argon well ahead of both Astra and Opus 5.5.These numbers matter because they sit closer to the work companies actually pay for: analyzing filings, drafting research memos, chaining tools, and producing usable outputs across long contexts.

- Advertisement -

Pure coding benchmarks remain competitive and sometimes favor rivals, yet the pattern across knowledge-work suites suggests Argon has been optimized for sustained, tool-using professional labor.

Long-context performance is another stated strength. The ability to sustain coherent generation and reasoning across a million tokens opens practical possibilities for reviewing large contract sets, multi-hour video, or sprawling codebases in a single pass. Google also reports leading results on long-video understanding and visual analysis of professional charts and documents.

Coding and the mixed picture

On DeepSWE v1.1, which tests realistic, multi-step software engineering, Argon posts 77.9 percent and claims a new state of the art. That result is meaningful for teams that want models capable of planning, editing and verifying code over extended sessions. At the same time, other coding and systems benchmarks show tighter or reversed rankings. Terminal-bench style evaluations and certain migration or infrastructure tasks still favor competitors in the numbers Google released.

The divergence is useful. It suggests that “best coding model” is no longer a single title. Different architectures and training mixtures excel at different slices of the software lifecycle. Argon’s profile leans toward long-horizon agency and professional tooling rather than pure competitive programming speed.

- Advertisement -

Cybersecurity as early proving ground

Google CEO Sundar Pichai introduces Gemini 4 Argon and outlines its early, responsible rollout.Image credit: News from Google

Google has given early access to cybersecurity defenders, and the company highlights at least one concrete result: the model identified a critical vulnerability in widely used healthcare software that earlier frontier systems had missed. On CWE-bench style vulnerability remediation tests, Argon ties for the top score.

“Importantly Argon has frontier safeguards and we are rolling it out responsibly – it’s with the US gov’t and going to a set of trusted cyber defenders through our Fairwind Program today. We’re going to make it available as soon as we can and as safely as we can. So hold tight, lots more coming, and you’re going to see us iterating rapidly.“, said Sundar Pichai, CEO, Google and Alphabet | Source

This early deployment choice is strategic. Security teams operate under high stakes and generate clear feedback loops. Success or failure in that domain will shape how quickly the model moves into broader enterprise use.

Controlled release and what comes next

Restricting initial access to trusted testers and security practitioners is consistent with the pattern of recent frontier releases. The risks of powerful models are no longer theoretical, and staged rollout gives both the developer and external experts time to observe failure modes before wider exposure. When paid API and Ultra subscribers receive access, the practical test will shift from benchmark tables to daily workflow integration: latency, tool reliability, cost per useful output, and the quality of long-context reasoning under real document loads.

- Advertisement -

Reading the leaderboard with care

Benchmark leadership is always provisional. The set of 19 tests Google chose emphasises the areas where Argon performs best. Independent evaluations on different suites, different agent harnesses, or adversarial conditions may paint a more varied picture. Absolute scores on several of the knowledge-work benchmarks remain modest even for the leader, which indicates that the tasks themselves are still hard for every current model. The gap between first and second place is informative, yet the distance from current performance to reliable autonomy is larger still.

What the results do show is a shift in emphasis. The competitive frontier is moving from general language fluency toward measurable economic utility: the ability to research, plan, use tools, and produce work product that professionals can trust or quickly revise. Argon’s reported strengths align with that shift.

A quieter kind of progress

Gemini 4 Argon branding as it appears on mobile. Image credit: Samuel Boivin | Nurphoto | Getty Images

Gemini 4 Argon does not arrive with claims of artificial general intelligence. It arrives with a table of numbers and a controlled access list. In the current phase of the field, that restraint is itself a form of progress. The model appears strongest where the work is structured, multi-step, and grounded in professional domains. It is less dominant where the tasks are narrower or more systems-oriented. That unevenness is honest. It gives users a clearer map of where to apply the system first and where to keep human oversight tight.

As the model moves from limited testing into paid hands, the decisive measurements will be less about which name sits at the top of any single leaderboard and more about whether the outputs shorten real work, surface real risks, and hold up under the messy conditions of daily use. For now, Google has put a new contender on the board, one that leads where professional knowledge work is measured and remains competitive elsewhere. The next chapters will be written by the people who actually put it to work.

- Advertisement -

members.title: Claude Code 2.1.289 closes a second route past its rm guard, and stable is four builds behind - MIXED Reality News

representative.headline: Claude Code 2.1.289 closes a second route past its rm guard, and stable is four builds behind - MIXED Reality News
representative.body: Claude Code 2.1.289 closes a second route past its rm guard, and stable is four builds behind    MIXED Reality News

articles.headline: Claude Code 2.1.289 closes a second route past its rm guard, and stable is four builds behind - MIXED Reality News
articles.body: Claude Code 2.1.289 closes a second route past its rm guard, and stable is four builds behind    MIXED Reality News

scored.body:
Claude Code 2.1.289 reached npm on October 3 at 20:12 UTC, and it closes a second route for a deletion command to slip past the permission check that is supposed to stop it. Anthropic's changelog describes the fix as "Fixed Bash deny and ask rules missing a command behind an environment variable prefix with an expanded value (e.g. TZ=\"$HOME\" rm -rf build) when the sandbox auto-allows commands".

Claude Code checks a shell command against its permission rules before it runs.

Anyone installing from the stable channel does not have that fix. At 23:58 UTC on October 4 the npm registry's dist-tags for the package still pointed stable at 2.1.285, while latest and next both sat on 2.1.289, four releases ahead.

Anthropic does not call either of the sandbox fixes a vulnerability. There is no CVE, no severity rating, and nothing in the changelog in Anthropic's own repository that says the path was ever used against anyone.

Both Bash fixes apply only under sandbox auto-allow

Anthropic scopes both of them to one situation. One applies "when the sandbox auto-allows commands", and the other covers "a Bash deny or ask rule being skipped under sandbox auto-allow when a bare variable assignment came before the command". Neither describes a default install with no sandbox in play.

A deny or ask rule matches on the command it expects to find at the front of the line, and an environment-variable assignment in front of it gives the shell something to read first. The previous release fixed the same guard against a different trick, where a bash -c wrapper got a dangerous rm past it, which we covered on October 3.

Managed machines get a third shell fix. A deny or ask rule on a nested part of a compound shell command was "not holding over a user-installed mod's approval on managed machines".

A plugin could rewrite an admin-installed server's sign-in text

The release also fixes something that has nothing to do with the shell. Anthropic records "Fixed a user-installed plugin being able to rewrite the descriptions of an organization-managed MCP server's sign-in tools".

Tool descriptions are the text a model reads to work out what a tool does and when to reach for it, so a description is instructions rather than decoration. An MCP server installed by an organisation's administrators is the half of that pairing a user is not supposed to be able to edit, and a sign-in tool is the one that asks for credentials. Anthropic says only that a user-installed plugin could change that text, not whether any plugin did.

File reads get a fix as well: Read deny rules were "not applying to files @-mentioned, changed, or selected in the IDE through a symlink". Five of the release's 27 fixes are permission or sandbox work, and most of the rest repair the plugin interface, including a freeze at launch when a plugin drew a border style the terminal does not know.

Stable has not moved since September 29

2.1.285 was published on September 29 at 17:32 UTC, and the four releases since have arrived at close to one a day: 2.1.286 on September 30 at 17:14 UTC, 2.1.287 on October 1 at 16:59 UTC, 2.1.288 on October 2 at 18:30 UTC and 2.1.289 on October 3 at 20:12 UTC. Anyone who installs from the stable tag gets none of the five permission fixes in the newest build.

That is a choice about release channels rather than a defect, and a conservative stable tag is the normal reason to have one. Anthropic publishes no schedule for promoting a build, so the gap is visible in the registry and nowhere else. The fix 2.1.289 flags for its own users is a smaller one: installed mods were not loading in the first session after an upgrade, which is the session in which someone would go looking for what changed.

articles.headline: Anthropic takes Claude inference live in India, opens path to regulated AI deployments - CRN Asia
articles.body: Anthropic takes Claude inference live in India, opens path to regulated AI deployments    CRN Asia

scored.body:
The move turns Anthropic’s August commitment to in-country processing into a live capability as Indian enterprises and services partners expand Claude deployments.

Anthropic has made Claude inference available in India through Amazon Bedrock, allowing customers to process inference requests within the country and giving regulated enterprises a local deployment option for workloads where data residency is a requirement.

Claude Opus 5, Claude Sonnet 5 and Claude Haiku 4.5 are now available through Amazon Bedrock’s India endpoint.

AWS says the India geographic cross-region inference profile keeps processing within its Mumbai and Hyderabad regions, allowing requests to move between the two India regions rather than being routed outside the country.

The launch turns Anthropic’s August commitment to bring Claude inference to India into a live capability.

At the time, the company said local inference was being developed in response to demand from Indian organisations, particularly those in banking, insurance, government and other regulated sectors where data sovereignty and compliance can determine whether AI workloads can move into production.

“In August, we committed to bringing Claude inference to India, and we are delivering on that promise,” said Irina Ghose, managing director, India, Anthropic. “Our customers, especially in regulated sectors and government, want to use Claude on their most critical work, with requests processed in the country. From today, they can.”

Ghose said Anthropic would continue to grow its India team and invest in local partnerships.

Local inference targets production workloads

The immediate significance of the India endpoint is the ability to keep Claude inference within Indian regions.

AWS says customers can use the India geographic profile across its Mumbai and Hyderabad regions, with prompts and outputs remaining within those regions. The architecture also allows Amazon Bedrock to use capacity across the two regions, rather than tying an application to the capacity of a single location.

That is relevant to customers where data residency is part of the requirements for production AI deployments. AWS has specifically identified financial services, healthcare and public-sector organisations among customers that can benefit from processing data within a defined geography.

Sandeep Dutta, president, AWS India and South Asia, said responsible AI adoption at scale has become a strategic requirement for regulated industries, with data residency often determining whether AI remains at the pilot stage or reaches production.

Claude deployments through Amazon Bedrock in India also come with audit trails and access controls for risk and compliance teams.

The customer response suggests that the value of local inference extends beyond regulatory requirements. Early customers, including Reliance and CRED, tested the capability in private preview, with customers also citing latency, performance and resilience.

Reliance said local inference gives it the performance, resilience and regulatory alignment required to move Claude into production areas across its ecosystem.

CRED pointed to the combination of performance and data governance requirements in the Indian financial sector, while Mahindra Group said keeping data and AI workloads within India would help it scale Claude across the group.

For Indian enterprises, the distinction is important. Claude was already accessible to customers in India through Amazon Bedrock, including through global cross-Region inference. The new geographic capability is specifically designed for customers that need inference processing to remain within India.

Anthropic moves from partner registrations to ecosystem build-out

The infrastructure launch also comes as Anthropic's partner strategy in India moves into its next phase.

When Anthropic announced its India expansion in August, it said India had recorded some of the highest registration numbers globally after the launch of the Claude Partner Network. Indian companies were already represented across the network’s Global Premier, Preferred and Select tiers.

That ecosystem has continued to develop. Anthropic held its first Claude Certification for Partners in Bengaluru in August, with up to 5,000 people certified through the programme.

The company is also positioning the partner network around enterprise AI implementation, with training, technical support and co-investment available to partners building Claude practices. Anthropic’s partner programme includes services partners supporting AI strategy, consulting and Claude implementation.

TCS is one of the most significant Indian partners in that ecosystem. The company describes itself as Anthropic’s Global Premier Partner and says it has one of the world’s largest pools of Claude-certified talent.

“As Anthropic’s Global Premier Partner, with one of the world’s largest pools of Claude certified talent, we see growing demand for enterprise-grade AI deployments in regulated industries,” said Amit Kapur, Chief AI & Services Transformation Officer, TCS. “Anthropic’s in-country inference capability in India is an important step in meeting evolving data residency and governance requirements.”

The services ecosystem extends beyond TCS. Anthropic says Infosys, Cognizant, LTM and LTTS are building Claude into client delivery worldwide.

TCS is rolling out Claude to 50,000 associates, while Infosys has established a dedicated Anthropic Centre of Excellence. Earlier, Anthropic also highlighted Cognizant’s use of Claude in client engagements across manufacturing, life sciences and insurance, while LTM and LTTS were integrating the technology into enterprise engineering platforms.

That makes the partner element more significant than a certification exercise. As enterprises move from model evaluation to production deployments, system integrators and services firms can provide the implementation, industry expertise and governance capabilities required around the underlying model.

Enterprise deployments broaden across India

Anthropic is also using the India launch to highlight how Claude adoption has expanded across sectors.

In financial services, Kotak Bank, Axis Bank, IndusInd Bank and NPCI are using Claude for engineering and employee productivity. NPCI is also building its AiNxt agentic AI platform with Claude.

Vijay Narayanan, head of innovation & AI, Kotak Bank, said in-country inference widens the options available to Indian banks and allows organisations with governance built into their AI platforms to adopt new capabilities responsibly.

Mahindra Group and Godrej Industries are among the large enterprises deploying Claude, while Reliance and CRED have also tested or deployed the technology across their organisations.

Godrej Industries said India-based inference gives it the regulatory alignment, performance and resilience needed to move Claude into production workflows.

Digital-native companies are using Claude in engineering and product environments. Freshworks runs Claude Code across its engineering organisation, while Swiggy says the technology is being used to address complex engineering problems rather than only automate routine tasks.

At the security level, the Data Security Council of India is using Claude Opus-powered agents to examine codebases, systems and infrastructure for vulnerabilities and to review agent flows, logic and security.

The wider customer base also includes Razorpay, Zomato, InVideo, Emergent, Rocket and Atlan.

The growing set of deployments gives Anthropic a larger base from which to take Claude into production workloads, while the availability of in-country inference removes one of the constraints faced by organisations handling sensitive data.

Anthropic’s India strategy is therefore moving into a different phase. The company had already established a local team, launched its partner network and begun building enterprise relationships.

With in-country inference now live, those pieces are being brought together around production deployments where local processing, enterprise governance and partner-led implementation are increasingly important.

Anthropic’s Bengaluru office, opened in February, is part of that broader investment. The company has said it will continue to expand its India team and local partnerships as adoption grows.

Published October 5, 2026 at 7:17 AM CDT

Artificial Intelligence is making waves, for better or worse, in Washington. As South Dakota prepares to elect its next US House Representative, what to do with this technology is front of mind.For Republican Marty Jackley, stressing that there is an AI race with China he doesn’t want America to lose, said there should be barriers.“As a country, we have to put guardrails in. Guardrails in respect to inappropriate use of AI, guardrails in respect to election integrity, and guardrails in respect to protecting consumers," Jackley said. "The attorney general received about 82,000 consumer complaints last year, and a lot of them were generated by scams associated with AI. We need to get to the bottom of it, Congress has a role.”For Democrat Nikki Gronli though, it’s not just an American concern, it’s a concern for the entire UN to work together on.“Yes, Congress has a role in regulation, getting those in the room to make sure we’re doing this in a successful and productive way," Gronli said. "Having (AI) let out can really be a Pandora's Box. We need not just our Congress working on it, but this needs to be a global ally situation.”Watch the full debate online.

The 2026 lectures, which will be held in Toronto this November, are co-founded by Nobel Laureate Professor Geoffrey Hinton, a renowned AI expert, and the AI Safety Foundation.

Hinton Lectures Poster

This partnership builds on Manulife's commitment to Responsible AI and support for informed dialogue on the responsible development of AI. Guided by its Responsible AI Principles, Manulife is focused on developing and deploying AI in a way that creates value for customers, colleagues and society while maintaining trust, managing risk, and promoting accountability.

"Our support for The Hinton Lectures™ reflects Manulife's commitment to advancing responsible AI," said Jodie Wallis, Manulife's Global Chief AI Officer. "AI is evolving quickly, and so are the questions around how we develop and use it responsibly. The Hinton Lectures bring together thoughtful perspectives from across research, industry and policy, and we're proud to be part of that conversation."

The Hinton Lectures™ are hosted by Professor Geoffrey Hinton and feature world-leading experts in AI safety. This year's keynote speaker is Paul Christiano, a leading expert in AI safety and alignment. The lecture series will take place November 9-11, 2026, at the Metro Toronto Convention Centre in Toronto. The events are open to the public and will also be livestreamed.Manulife senior leaders will participate throughout the series, delivering opening remarks and sharing perspectives on responsible AI, governance, trust and innovation alongside leaders from research, industry and policy."We're pleased to welcome Manulife back to The Hinton Lectures, this year as our presenting partner," said Ankesh Chandaria, CEO of the AI Safety Foundation. "Their expanded support reflects a shared commitment to advancing thoughtful conversations about the responsibilities that come with AI. We're proud to partner with an organization that is helping drive the responsible adoption of AI and bring these important discussions to a broader audience."Manulife has been actively investing in and scaling AI capabilities since 2016. In the past four years, the firm has significantly increased the value enabled through AI by expanding its AI solutions portfolio and increasing efficiency through data and AI platform investments. Manulife has been named the number one life insurance company for AI maturity for the second consecutive year, and ranks among the top insurers overall in the 2026 Evident AI Index for Insurance. More information on Manulife's AI progress can be found on Manulife.com/AI.The public can register for tickets or the livestream online at HintonLectures.com. The event is organized by the AI Safety Foundation and hosted by Professor Geoffrey Hinton.For additional details on the 2026 Hinton Lectures, including this year's distinguished lecturer announcement, please see the AI Safety Foundation's announcement here. About Manulife   Manulife Financial Corporation is a leading international financial services provider, headquartered in Toronto, Canada. Anchored in our ambition to be the number one choice for customers, we operate as Manulife across Canada and Asia, and primarily as John Hancock in the United States, providing financial advice, insurance and health solutions for individuals, groups and businesses. Through Manulife Wealth & Asset Management, we offer global investment solutions, financial advice, and retirement plan services to individuals, institutions, and retirement plan members worldwide. At the end of 2025, we had more than 37,000 employees, over 106,000 agents, and thousands of distribution partners, serving over 37 million customers with operations across 25 markets globally. We trade as 'MFC' on the Toronto, New York, and Philippine stock exchanges, and under '945' on the Hong Kong stock exchange. Not all offerings are available in all jurisdictions. For additional information, please visit manulife.com.Media ContactEmily English (647) 544-2800 [email protected]SOURCE Manulife Financial Corporation
